news.title: Democrats Fear Their 'Blue Wave' May Have Crested Too Early
news.text: Democrats are entering the final stretch of the midterm campaign with numbers that look almost too good to be true. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, has declared that his party has "the wind in our sails." House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, also a New York Democrat, told reporters on Sunday that they "are poised to take back the majority." Democratic Senate candidates now lead polling averages from Texas to Alaska, and in states President Donald Trump carried two years ago. But for many inside the party, the confidence comes with a warning attached. Midterms are, of course, a different contest. Voter turnout changes, Trump is not on the ballot, and history tends to favor the party out of power. Democrats are leading Republicans in almost every generic congressional ballot average. Still, with fewer than four weeks until Election Day and early voting already underway, Democratic leaders, strategists, and veterans of past wave elections are cautioning against the kind of overconfidence they say hurt the party last time. "I will tell you that the antidote to overconfidence is the [20]24 election," Former North Dakota Senator Heidi Heitkamp told Newsweek. "People saw this in 24 and said it's not over till it's over." Heitkamp, a Democrat who lost her reelection bid in the 2018 wave, believes the defeat itself is what will keep her party from repeating it, but warned Democrats against reading too much into their lead. "I think that the Democrats shouldn't get too cozy about saying that people are selecting the Democratic Party," she said. "I think they're rejecting the party of Donald Trump." The Wind in Their Sails The Cook Political Report, widely considered the gold standard for nonpartisan race ratings, moved 18 House races toward Democrats last week. Party officials privately expect Democrats to win back the House, and the Senate, once seen as safer terrain for Republicans, now looks like a tossup. But some top Democrats are less sure the polls can be trusted. Former President Barack Obama warned donors at a fundraiser for Senate Democrats on Wednesday that narrow leads could evaporate. "All these races that are showing we've got a two- or three-point lead or it's a tossup, we could end up losing all of them by two points," Obama said. "It's within the margin of error." The House may be slipping out of reach for Republicans, but the Senate is still up for grabs. The GOP holds a 53-47 majority, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. A 50-50 split would leave Vice President JD Vance with the tie-breaking vote. Their clearest openings are in North Carolina and Maine. In North Carolina, former Governor Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley 50.9 percent to 41.1 percent in the FiftyPlusOne polling average. In Maine, the only Republican-held seat in a state former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024, Democrat Troy Jackson leads Senator Susan Collins 49 percent to 46.7 percent. Beyond those two, the path to a majority runs through states Trump won comfortably. Former Senator Sherrod Brown leads Republican Senator Jon Husted in Ohio, 47.7 percent to 44 percent. In Texas, state Representative James Talarico leads Attorney General Ken Paxton 48.4 percent to 45.1 percent, and in Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Senator Dan Sullivan 48.9 percent to 46 percent. Iowa and Kansas are closer still. Democrat Josh Turek holds a lead of less than a point over Representative Ashley Hinson in Iowa, while in Kansas, a race Cook just moved into its toss-up column, Democrat Adam Hamilton leads Senator Roger Marshall by 1.4 points. In Nebraska, Senator Pete Ricketts is ahead of independent Dan Osborn by less than a point. Democrats also have seats to defend. Progressive Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, 48.1 percent to 44.4 percent, and Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan leads by more than 3 points in Minnesota against Michele Tafoya, Republicans' best pickup opportunity. In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff holds a lead of about 9 points against Representative Mike Collins. Most of those margins sit inside the range Obama and other Democrats have warned about. "Winning seats in red states during an era of hyper-partisanship will not be easy. Democrats have momentum, and the floor seems to be dropping out beneath the president's polling, but no Democrat should get comfortable," Doug Gordon, a Democratic strategist and co-founder of UpShift Strategies, told Newsweek. "Every Democrat should be running as if they're 10 points behind." The Ghost of October 2024 The numbers from two years ago still haunt party strategists. Harris led Trump by an average of 3.6 points across national polls conducted in September 2024. October polls cut that edge to 1.7 points, and the RealClearPolitics average of surveys taken after October 9 showed her ahead by less than a point. The battlegrounds moved the same way. September polling had Harris leading in four of the seven swing states, while October surveys showed her ahead in just one. On Election Day, Trump carried all seven battlegrounds and won the national popular vote by about 1.5 points. "Polls considerably underestimated Donald Trump and other Republicans on the ticket with him in 2016, 2020, and, to a slightly lesser extent, in 2024," statistician and election analyst Nate Silver wrote this past weekend. Silver added that polls in the two Trump-era midterms, 2018 and 2022, were essentially unbiased. For a party leaning on narrow margins, the difference matters. Recent polling averages found margin-of-error races in Michigan, Texas, Maine and Iowa, and a modest polling miss in either direction could reshape several of the contests that will decide the Senate. Gordon told Newsweek that while the winds are favorable, the party needs to temper its optimism. "Election Day is not three weeks away," he said. "Election Day is every day for the next three weeks. Early voting is already happening, and more than 2 million votes have already been cast." Even Jeffries, who has compared this year to the 2018 wave, when Democrats regained control of the House, cautioned last Sunday that "anything and everything" is possible and urged Democrats to stay focused. Heitkamp said the political landscape is different this time around. Unlike Democrats in 2024, candidates are not running with the baggage of defending the Biden administration, which she said gives them more room to define themselves on their own terms. "The Democratic candidate has an opportunity to define what they would do without having to answer for an administration that was not viewed favorably by the voters in their district," she said. A Different Kind of Wave The last two midterms in which Democrats surged against an unpopular Republican president, 2006 and 2018, came when voters still felt relatively confident about the economy. The Iraq War dragged down President George W. Bush in 2006, and college-educated suburbanites abandoned Trump’s party in 2018. This year, the economy itself is the problem. Gas prices and interest rates are up, inflation has refused to ease, and Trump’s tariffs have driven up prices in rural America. The University of Michigan’s Index of Consumer Sentiment has fallen 33 percent since Trump returned to office in January 2025. In May, it hit its lowest point since monthly tracking began in 1952. Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at the centrist think tank Third Way, said the souring economy is what separates this cycle from a typical midterm swing. “I don’t think Democrats are peaking too early,” Kessler told Newsweek. “This feels like a gathering storm that could drown a lot of Republicans who thought they were in safe seats.” Kessler, who said this is his 19th election cycle in Washington, has seen three others like it: 1994, 2006 and 2010. Two favored Republicans and one favored Democrats. In each, he said, voters were fed up with Washington, pessimistic about the economy and down on their own finances. “In the past, voters never really liked Trump all that much but at least they could say, ‘well, the economy is good,’” he said. “No one thinks the economy is good today and they rightfully blame the President because the tariffs and Iran War were his ideas alone.” Heitkamp sees the same frustration. Voters have been patient with the administration, she said, but they do not see it confronting the cost of living, housing and inflation with any urgency. “Instead, they hear stories about, you know, the reflecting pool and the east wing,” she said, referring to Trump’s renovation projects in Washington, including the demolition of the White House’s East Wing to build a ballroom. Costas Panagopoulos, a political scientist at Northeastern University, disputed the notion that Democrats have lost momentum. What matters, he said, is whether support is durable or merely superficial. "Democrats remain highly energized, with strong enthusiasm for defeating Republicans and a deep motivation to turn out on Election Day," he said. Is There Room for a GOP Comeback? Republicans can read the map. Trump rallied Monday in Grand Island, Nebraska, a state he won by 20 points in 2024, to shore up Ricketts, and stumped last week in Oklahoma, which he carried by 34. GOP groups are also spending to protect incumbents in Kansas and South Carolina. “I think the cake is baked, minus some external event which in this world is entirely possible,” Alex Patton, a Republican strategist with Ozean Media, told Newsweek. “The GOP isn’t going to solve inflation, the war, gas prices in the next few weeks.” Patton said Trump’s approval ratings will not jump 20 points before November's election. He added that Republican efforts to convince voters the economy is strong land “flat and out of touch.” The party has fallen back on fear to turn out its base, he said, “and even that appears to be failing.” Kessler put it more bluntly. “We’re less than a month from Election Day and Republicans are worried about losing a Senate race in Kansas,” he said. “It’s batten down the hatches time for the GOP.” A sweeping Democratic victory is still far from guaranteed. Republicans hold a large money advantage, with MAGA Inc. and other GOP groups outspending Democrats in every crucial Senate race. In Texas alone, Republican super PACs have directed more than $150 million to Paxton, compared with $4 million from Democratic super PACs for Talarico. “Is all lost for Republicans? No,” Kessler said. “They have several things going for them, including a huge money advantage and some underperforming Democrats in key states like Michigan and Maine in the Senate races." The two races Kessler mentions are key for the Democratic hopes to regain the chamber. In Michigan, a seat Democrats must hold, El-Sayed has struggled to open a meaningful lead over Rogers, with most polling putting him ahead 50 percent to 49 percent among likely voters. Before the August primary, several polls showed the Republican beating the progressive former public health official. In Maine, meanwhile, Democrats lost valuable time after a messy nomination fight. Oyster farmer Graham Platner forced Governor Janet Mills out of the race in April and went on to win the June primary, but he withdrew in July following a sexual assault allegation. The state party then nominated former state Senate President Troy Jackson on July 25. Jackson now leads Collins by just over 2 points. Then, there is the Democratic brand itself, which remains a drag on the party even as voters sour on Trump. Democrats are still underwater nationally, posting a 44 percent favorable and 55 percent unfavorable rating in a recent Fox News poll and a 38 percent favorable, 58 percent unfavorable rating in a recent Wall Street Journal survey. Dissatisfaction extends beyond the party's broader image: Schumer and Jeffries have also struggled to win over voters, including many on the left. Patton sees no sign Democrats are coasting. But he would treat any race within 10 points as unfinished. “You gotta run through the tape and leave nothing to chance,” he said. Heitkamp has a similar conclusion. Two years after watching her party’s lead slip away, she said Democrats are more worried about history repeating itself than about anything else. “I don’t think that there will be kind of an overconfidence,” she said. “I think there will be a huge push to push through the tape at the end.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jason Lemon and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Democrats head into the midterms’ final stretch with numbers that look too good to be true. Many in the party see it as a warning.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Kamala Harris Is the Shadow Incumbent of 2028
news.text: Kamala Harris has yet to announce a 2028 presidential campaign, but Gavin Newsom's declaration that he would stay out if she runs has exposed her peculiar standing in Democratic politics: a former nominee with no office, no campaign and enough influence to make other ambitious Democrats plan around her. Harris is the shadow incumbent of 2028. The former vice president may be the only politician in America enjoying some of the privileges of incumbency without having won the presidency. Other Democrats must account for her ambitions before pursuing their own, while she remains free to decide whether she wants another shot at the job. It's a rather enviable position for someone who lost the last election. The arrangement has a catch, though, given the strange position that Harris occupies. She was the party's most recent presidential nominee, served four years in the White House and can plausibly argue that 2024 was an exceptionally poor test of her political abilities: 107 days to rescue a candidacy she had never expected to inherit under circumstances no presidential nominee would willingly choose. But the same resume that gives her a claim on the party's future ties her to its immediate past. Democrats who want to turn the page on the Biden years must first contend with the woman who spent four years at his side and then lost the election to succeed him. Newsom Has Already Made His Calculation In September, Newsom, California's Democratic governor, told CNN, "I wouldn't run if she ran." He described a contest between the two Californians (Harris served as the state's attorney general and U.S. senator before the White House) as "mutual assured destruction," arguing that their rivalry would benefit other candidates. Newsom's calculation is obvious: they come from the same state, have spent decades cultivating overlapping donors and political allies, and would risk dividing their own California base while rivals from elsewhere benefited. Why spend millions fighting someone whose supporters you may eventually need? By promising to stay out if she runs, Newsom has effectively given Harris a say in his political future. But Newsom has specific reasons to avoid Harris that other potential candidates don't. A governor from Kentucky or Maryland has a different political base and considerably less to lose from challenging her. Newsom's deference may therefore reveal more about the peculiarities of California politics than about Harris' command of the Democratic Party. Elsewhere, Harris' influence takes a different form. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro has left open the possibility of a 2028 run, while Illinois Governor JB Pritzker has established a $20 million political action committee and visited battleground states. Neither has promised to defer to Harris, and both are pursuing their political futures while she considers hers. So Newsom has made his plans contingent on her decision, while others are moving ahead, potentially competing against her. Either way, her potential candidacy is part of the calculation. Veteran Democratic strategist Joe Trippi told Newsweek: "Potential candidates in 2028 would be foolish to not include her possible entry into the race and how it might impact their fundraising, support and messaging." And that's the difference between Harris' influence and her actual power: she can complicate other candidates' plans without necessarily stopping them. As Trippi put it: "No one, including Vice President Harris, will get a cleared field." The Coalition Harris Could Keep The stronger argument for Harris' unusual standing comes from the voters who helped make her the nominee in 2024. Pew Research Center found that 83 percent of Black voters supported Harris in the 2024 general election. President Donald Trump's share rose from 8 percent in 2020 to 15 percent in 2024. In an interview with Newsweek, Reverend Al Sharpton said Harris holds a special place among Black Democrats, many of whom believe her abbreviated campaign deserves another hearing. "I think that she has a unique special standing," Sharpton said, pointing to her vote total and the 107 days she had to campaign. Sharpton said Harris received the strongest reception by far at his National Action Network convention. He also described a distinction he was hearing from voters: they would consider other candidates if Harris declined to run, but would be reluctant to abandon her if she entered. That leaves other Democrats with a delicate task: they can cultivate Harris' former supporters, but may struggle to convert goodwill into commitments while her intentions remain unresolved. Sharpton singled out Maryland Governor Wes Moore and Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear as alternatives attracting attention. Sharpton said Beshear's ability to win twice in a Republican state and his religious language resonate with some Black voters. Still, Sharpton cautioned against assuming Harris could simply inherit their support. "I think she will have a certain amount that will go to her automatically but she still should work for it, not take anything for granted," he said. The Limits of Harris' Shadow Incumbency Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has offered the clearest indication that Harris' influence has limits. Asked about her political future, the New York Democrat told The New York Times: "I don't think that my decisions would come down to deference." Some Democrats facing voters in Republican-leaning states have gone further, treating an association with Harris as a potential electoral liability. Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton said Harris should stay away from his campaign, arguing that her presence would hurt his chances of attracting voters. In Alaska, Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign rejected an unsolicited fundraising appeal from Harris, which would have split donations between Peltola and Harris' political organization. Both episodes point to the other side of Harris' shadow incumbency: the same political identity that gives her influence over the 2028 field can make her a liability for Democrats trying to win elsewhere. There is an obvious reason for their caution. Harris lost to Trump in 2024, 312 electoral votes to 226. Her 107-day campaign gives her a credible argument that she deserves another chance, but it hardly obliges Democrats to give her one. Ocasio-Cortez's refusal to defer, along with resistance from candidates in Kansas and Alaska, reminds us that the shadow incumbent's authority ultimately depends on other Democrats choosing to recognize it. For Harris, the calculation is therefore delicate. The longer she waits, the longer she can enjoy the advantages of a prospective candidacy without facing the scrutiny of an actual one. But the party cannot wait indefinitely. At Sharpton's April convention, Harris said she was considering another run. If she enters, Democrats will have to decide whether her defeat was due to exceptional circumstances or a reason to choose someone else. If she stays out, candidates who have been courting her former supporters can pursue them more openly. Until then, Harris occupies an unusual position: she can influence the contest without participating. The question is how long other Democrats will allow her that luxury.
news.summary: Gavin Newsom would step aside, while other Democrats are keeping their distance. Harris' influence over 2028 comes with a catch.
news.author: Anna Rahmanan

news.title: Anthony Scaramucci On 'Low Artist' Trump, Misjudged 'Ass-Kissing' And What Really Got Him Fired
news.text:
NEW YORK — Anthony Scaramucci is searching for a video on his phone. A clip that will set the record straight. I’m reading him a quotation from the only White House press conference he gave as President Donald Trump’s communications chief, a period in his life he calls, in his new book, “the 11-day fiasco.”

“I’ve seen this guy throw a dead spiral through a tire,” Scaramucci told a reporter from the briefing room podium, in 2017, when putting on some razzle dazzle in the early-ish days of Trump 1.0. “I’ve seen him at Madison Square Garden with a top coat on, he’s standing in the key and he’s hitting foul shots and swishing them. He sinks 3-foot putts.” (The official White House record was later corrected to “30-foot putts.”)

“I gotta show it to you,” he says, nine years later, while talking at a Manhattan members-only club. “Here we go.”

It’s a video of Trump, in 1992, at a baseball stadium in Buffalo, New York, for a charity event, wearing a notably un-Trumpian plaid shirt. (Scaramucci: “He’s not a fashionable guy.”) Girlfriend Marla Maples is in tow.

Then, history appears to vindicate “The Mooch.” Surrounded by NFL legends, the real estate mogul fires a football through the smallest of holes roughly 20 yards away: more or less, a dead spiral through a tire. The crowd goes nuts.

“I didn’t make it up,” says Scaramucci, who insists he was also at Madison Square Garden for the foul-shot-in-a-top-coat moment. “I don’t have the tape of that,” he adds, sadly.

“They always broke my balls about that,” he says, referencing the mockery he faced for the claims of Trump’s sporting prowess. “But you know what? I saw it.”

Scaramucci does concede, however, that the now infamous peroration was “a gigantic ass-kissing move.” Not that the fawning press conference impressed the big man, who for one day at least was not the center of attention. There was a new showman in town. “He didn’t like it,” Scaramucci says. “One-man show, one spotlight.”

“I shouldn’t have done that,” he says of the exercise in Trump flattery. “Add that to my mistakes, my man.”

Mistakes — his own, but mainly those made by political leaders over the last 30 years — are the centerpiece of his new book, “All The Wrong Moves: How Three Catastrophic Decisions Led to the Rise of Trump,” which attempts to outline “what came before Trump to make Trumpism possible,” and paints a grim picture of the threats to democracy today.

As anyone who has tracked his career over the last decade knows, the Anthony Scaramucci who simped for Trump in the White House for less than two weeks — said to be a modern-day record — and the one who wrote this damning book are appreciably different people.

Scaramucci was once a Trump acolyte who believed the TV personality-turned-insurgent politician was the answer to a malaise created by an out-of-touch bipartisan elite. In the book, he writes how Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told Scaramucci that “I reminded him of his dad, Fred Trump.”

“I said whatever was on my mind; I was classic New York,” he writes of why Trump liked him. The brash Long Island hedge funder, who rocked up to Washington, D.C., in a riot of aviator shades and expensive threads, appeared well-suited to be Trump’s emissary on The Hill.

Now, he is one of the president’s fiercest critics. Scaramucci’s podcast, “The Rest Is History: US.”, co-hosted by the BBC’s Katty Kay, is a smash hit, especially in the UK. Audiences attending an inaugural North America tour this month are likely to hear more unvarnished views on his former boss. 

Scaramucci, 62, who returned to Wall Street after his brief foray in the capital, sees the big mistakes that cleared the way for Trump through the prism of economics. The “money point of view” of history, he calls it.

Put simply, it started with President Bill Clinton’s embrace of trade with China that hurt American workers “deeply, quickly and permanently,” and continued when President George W. Bush cut taxes at the same time as he funded elongated wars in the Middle East. The last gateway to Trump was President Barack Obama bailing out Wall Street after the 2008 crash while main street faced ruin.

The result? Americans, whose wages were crushed while the “fat cats” got fatter, decided to “hire an orange wrecking ball.” Twice.

The book also details his own “catastrophically stupid decision” to work for Trump, first in the 2016 transition team and later as director of communications, as there were “things that he was doing that I morally equivocated on and overlooked.”

“Jeb Bush told me not to. Mitt Romney told me not to,” he says of the two senior Republicans he’d previously raised funds for. “George W. Bush told me not to.”

“But I smelled power, and I got my ego involved,” he adds.

Aside from that bombastic press conference, Scaramucci’s ill-fated 11 days as the president’s media gatekeeper included mopping up after Trump gave a bizarre address to the Boy Scouts of America, which included anecdotes about yacht parties involving “New York’s hottest people.”

“At the Jamboree, Trump speaks for twenty-nine minutes and says almost nothing that’s not completely insane,” Scaramucci writes in the book.

In person, he recalls the horror of standing backstage listening to Trump “lacing his speech with impromptu sexual innuendo to 12-year-old boys,” and senior White House aide Kellyanne Conway explaining this was his problem to deal with.

“And I was like, ’I’m not cleaning that up. I’m giving that to [new press secretary] Sarah [Huckabee Sanders], man. That’s a big elephant shit right there.”

The Boy Scouts speech in West Virginia was the same day his wife — who was in the process of divorcing him — was giving birth to their son in New York, and there was no way of getting back in time. “I mean, it was a really bad day for me,” he reflects.

“Now, some people push back,” he continues. “Oh, you know, you turned [working for Trump] into a great podcast and you did this, did that. It sucked! I’m not gonna sugarcoat it.”

He patched up his marriage and rebuilt his business. But the public humiliation — “getting ripped up by all the late-night comedians” and being “lit up by the fucking ‘Saturday Night Live’ ... calling me human cocaine” — still seems to sting.

He says his downfall came not, as many think, after being caught off-guard in an interview with The New Yorker and saying, among other things, that “I’m not [Trump chief strategist] Steve Bannon, I’m not trying to suck my own cock.” In fact, the president was apparently amused by “one of the funniest fucking things ever said from the fucking White House.”

“You think Trump really gave a shit?” he asks now of the Bannon jibe.

The end, he writes, was fueled by something less profanity-strewn: telling Trump he couldn’t veto the Russia sanctions bill over election interference that Republicans had passed. In any case, after mere days, Scaramucci was fired from the White House by Trump’s new chief of staff, John Kelly. He had “bombed so cataclysmically,” he writes.

Scaramucci initially stayed loyal to Trump. But, by 2019, he recognized Trump “wasn’t ever going to be a blue-collar president. He was exploiting the suffering of the people for his own narcissistic and malevolent ends,” he writes in the book.

Given how Trump expects loyalty, blowback to Scaramucci’s decision to be publicly critical of the president was perhaps inevitable. He’s had that. But Scaramucci points out that Trump “attacked me first,” and then “went after my wife on Twitter, which really caused the fight.” He says MAGA World people, who he was still close to, told Trump he “went over the line with me.”

“By the way, let me tell you something,” he says now. “If Donald Trump attacks your wife, you better back your fucking wife up, OK?”

Trump, he says, is “a low, low artist.”

Despite the feud and his conversion to Never Trumpism, some people are “still mad at me that I went to work for Donald Trump, even though I had my comeuppance.”

“There is a group of people in this country that I will be forever tarred and feathered and tattooed. And then there’s another group of people like, ‘Hey, man, the fucking guy made a mistake. He was honest about it, and he tried to pull us out of it.’”

Does he feel guilty about enabling Trump? “I do feel guilty about it, but I feel like I was exonerated,” he says, countering that he helped President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris to try to stop him. “I feel that I did my duty. And if you’re really being honest, it is the failure of the Democratic Party that he exists, right?”

In the book, Scaramucci argues the second Trump administration’s goal is to have “no effective restraint on the presidency — a kind of ‘soft’ dictatorship” similar to strongman leaders such as Victor Orbán in Hungary and Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

“Democracy has been overcome elsewhere. There’s no magical, existential reason that democracy isn’t being overcome here,” he writes. He also says in the book that “we’ll have to be ready for the next Trump” if we survive this one, and tells me the word from the rubber-chicken dinner fundraising circuit is that Vice President JD Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) are lining themselves up to be his successor, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio may sit 2028 out.

His suggested cure involves codifying many of the “norms” that have failed to constrain Trump, and he advocates for a future president who has the “willpower, guts, and political smarts to drive a stake through” the heart of the Trump playbook. He doesn’t know who that is yet. Also: the Republican Party has to die. “The GOP already has. It’s time for the funeral,” he writes.

In person, he says he doesn’t want to be entirely cynical. He reaches for a suitably Scaramuccian analogy to suggest the president’s current unpopularity, fueled by the Iran war, could mean the midterms are fatal for Trump, vanquishing any fears that he’ll cling to power after 2028 — a kind of Forever Trump, where he refuses to leave the White House despite term limits, which Scaramucci raises as a possibility in the book.

The political cycle means Americans are “stuck with the guy for four years.” But at the end of year two, a “customer complaint aisle” opens: “I believe that he’ll probably get hit with a tsunami of complaints, which could potentially knock him out of business.”
news.summary:
Anthony Scaramucci, the former Donald Trump acolyte-turned-loud critic and podcaster: “I smelled power, and I got my ego involved.”NEW YORK — Anthony Scaramucci is searching for a video on his phone. A clip that will set the record straight. I’m reading him a quotation from the only White House press conference he gave as President Donald Trump’s communications chief, a period in his life he calls, in his new book, “the 11-day fiasco.”

“I’ve seen this guy throw a dead spiral through a tire,” Scaramucci told a reporter from the briefing room podium, in 2017, when putting on some razzle dazzle in the early-ish days of Trump 1.0. “I’ve seen him at Madison Square Garden with a top coat on, he’s standing in the key and he’s hitting foul shots and swishing them. He sinks 3-foot putts.” (The official White House record was later corrected to “30-foot putts.”)

“I gotta show it to you,” he says, nine years later, while talking at a Manhattan members-only club. “Here we go.”

It’s a video of Trump, in 1992, at a base

news.title: Trump Says He Could Say 'Stupidest Things' as Polls Show GOP Concern
news.text: President Donald Trump joked that supporters would applaud “the stupidest things” during a Tennessee rally on Saturday, underscoring his confidence in his grip on the GOP base even as polls suggest some of his 2024 voters want Republican candidates to distance themselves from him ahead of November's midterms. Trump repeatedly cast himself as the driving force behind Republican success and urged supporters to turn out for the midterms at a campaign rally for Tennessee Republicans Senator Bill Hagerty and gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn. "I'm very popular. I really am," Trump told the Clarksville crowd. What the Polls Show on Trump Trump's comments come as new polling points to potential enthusiasm challenges for Republicans despite Trump's continued dominance within the party. A POLITICO/PF Global poll published Thursday found that 26 percent of voters who backed Trump in 2024 believe Republican candidates should break with the president in order to win in November. Separately, a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted between September 30 and October 5 found that just 30 percent of Trump's 2024 voters described themselves as "very enthusiastic" about voting in this year's midterm elections, compared with 48 percent of voters who backed former Vice President Kamala Harris. In addition, a Pew Research Center poll released October 8 found that Trump’s approval among voters who backed him in 2024 had fallen to 67 percent, down from 75 percent in July, 83 percent at the beginning of 2026 and 95 percent early in his second term. Thirty-one percent of his 2024 voters now disapprove of his job performance. Republican strategist Charlie Gerow told Newsweek this week that some of the findings raised the stakes for the party's turnout efforts, while predicting the enthusiasm gap could narrow as Republicans focus on the prospect of Democrats gaining power. "The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what's going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections," Gerow said. The polling nevertheless points to erosion rather than a wholesale break with Trump. A series of summer surveys found his approval among Republicans remained around 80 percent or higher, including 86 percent in an August Emerson poll, 80 percent in an Economist/YouGov survey and 80 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in late July and early August. The latest Pew Research Center survey found 77 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents remained confident in his decision-making on immigration, a hallmark issue of his 2024 campaign. Trump dismissed suggestions that he has become a political liability for Republican candidates, using part of his Tennessee speech to rebut media commentary he said he had seen while traveling aboard Air Force One. Referencing television analysts discussing about battleground states, Trump added: "The guy said, 'Well, I don't know. The Republicans are going to lose because Trump is so unpopular.' I'm very popular." He later argued that Republican candidates benefit from their association with him. "You'll win because I am popular," Trump said. "We're common sense. We want borders. We want low taxes." The president also touted the strong reception he receives at rallies, telling supporters that appearing before crowds of loyal backers makes campaigning easier. "There's such love in these rooms," Trump said. "I could say the stupidest things, and you'd clap." Trump immediately qualified the remark, adding: "But we don't say the stupidest things. We say things of common sense." Newsweek has reached out to the White House via email on Saturday night for comment. Trump's Tennessee Talking Points Throughout the nearly two-hour appearance, Trump repeatedly stressed the connection between his political brand and Republican electoral success. At one point, he questioned why he was campaigning in a state he has comfortably carried in previous elections. He has been in Texas and New York in recent days, trying to put his weight behind close races there. "What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?" Trump asked, noting that he expects Hagerty, Blackburn and other Republican candidates to win. "I don't have to campaign here, and I win." Trump said he chose to campaign in Tennessee anyway because he wanted to thank supporters in a state that had backed him repeatedly. "Sometimes it's nice to go to a place where you don't have to be, but you're there to say thank you to the great people that elected you three separate times." Trump spent part of the speech attacking transgender inclusion in women's sports, arguing it had become a winning political issue for Republicans and suggesting Democrats were out of step with voters on the issue. He also revived complaints about Canadian trade practices and riffed about renaming geographic landmarks, suggesting Lake Ontario could become "Lake America" and joking that the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean could one day be known as the "Trump Ocean." Trump also promoted his proposed "$5,000 Trump dividend," arguing tariff revenue would allow Republicans to send direct payments to Americans if the party retains control of Congress. Why an Enthusiasm Gap Matters for Midterms A recent CBS News/YouGov poll offered a broader look at the potential implications of who feels compelled to turn out to vote in the November 3 midterms. Its Battleground Tracker estimates Democrats currently have an advantage in the fight for a narrow House majority, citing opposition to the Trump administration's policies and a Republican base that is less likely to turn out. Republicans may struggle to hold their edge in Congress if their voters don't turn out, according to the poll. In the Reuters/Ipsos survey, 52 percent of respondents said a candidate's stance on the cost of living would be the most important factor in their congressional vote. And the CBS poll also found that many voters felt the administration had not focused enough on lowering food costs. Republicans who think Trump isn't focused on prices were less likely to say they would definitely vote, according to the poll. The findings suggest a two-part challenge for Republicans involving addressing an issue voters say matters to their decision and persuading less-motivated supporters that the election is worth turning out for. For Democrats, the polls suggests to an opportunity to rally turnout in competitive races. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. For more analysis from us on the numbers shaping U.S. politics and the 2026 midterms, sign up for Newsweek's Midterms Monitor newsletter.
news.summary: President Donald Trump tells Tennessee crowd that he will carry the Republican Party through the midterms.
news.author: Jennifer Radcliffe

news.title: President Trump casts long shadow over California campaigns
news.text:
Even before Donald Trump’s confusing gaffe Monday night in Nebraska about Iran bombing Los Angeles and San Diego, the president was looming large over nearly every hotly contested California election campaign.

In one Southern California race, Trump’s long shadow produced a disjointed two-step. Rep. Ken Calvert is attacking fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim for her anti-Trump stances, even as a Calvert-aligned PAC sent Democratic voters in the district mailers playing up her support for and from Trump.

Confused? That’s understandable. Under the new map, Calvert’s 41st Congressional District in Southern California was redrawn as a solidly Democratic seat, so the 33-year incumbent chose to run in the neighboring 40th, which stretches from the eastern edge of Orange County into a large chunk of western Riverside County.

That move set up the cycle’s strangest California race: Calvert versus Kim in a solidly Republican district that Trump carried by 12 points. It has been one of the nastiest campaigns in the country, with both sides fighting over who is more loyal to Trump. During the primary, a pro-Calvert super PAC, Americans 4 Security, spent $2.9 million on anti-Kim ads. Calvert has called Kim a “backstabbing RINO” and a “Trump-traitor,” and the PAC’s ads paint her as a liberal who hates Trump, citing her past vote to censure the president while ignoring her votes against Democrats’ efforts to impeach him.

Yet the same pro-Calvert super PAC sent two deliberately deceptive mailers to Democrats, playing up Kim’s pro-MAGA record. One showed a photo of a smiling Kim with the words “Young Kim, 100% with Trump,” and “a proven fighter who will stand with President Trump to deliver a bold American First Agenda.”

The goal was obvious: Turn off Democratic households and discourage party crossover support for Kim.

Kim answered with an ad focused on Calvert’s old scandals. It cites a 2009 Orange County Register editorial that ranked him among the most corrupt members of Congress, calls him swampy and sleazy, and revives a 1994 Los Angeles Times story about police catching him with a prostitute in his car. The ad ends by calling Calvert a “sleazebag.”

For all their fighting over Trump, both Calvert and Kim carefully avoided the furor over his Iran comments early this week, even as the remarks set off a raging debate on social media and in campaigns across the state. The timing could hardly have been worse for Republicans: The comments landed just as most California voters began receiving their mail-in ballots.

Speaking before a cheering crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, Monday night, Trump defended his war with Iran with a line that landed hard 1,500 miles west: “Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego.” The White House defended the line, saying the president was clearly warning about what Iran could do with a nuclear weapon, not encouraging it.

Although the explanation clearly fits the context of the president’s remarks, it didn’t satisfy everyone in his own party. By Tuesday morning, the Republican running in Southern California’s most closely watched open House seat was publicly breaking with him.

Jim Desmond, a San Diego County supervisor and Navy veteran who is the GOP nominee in the redrawn 48th District, said he “vehemently” disapproved of what the president said. The district is currently represented by retiring Rep. Darrell Issa.

Desmond’s quick distancing is a measure of how worried Republicans are about Trump’s waning popularity even in precincts he carried in previous elections – a dynamic playing out beyond California’s borders as well.

The newly drawn 48th district is a hook-shaped swath that includes areas in San Diego and Riverside counties, including around Vista, San Marcos, Palm Springs, and Temecula. The current configuration changed a 12-point Republican voter registration advantage to a 4-point Democratic lead. That, of course, was done by design. Late last year, state Democrats redrew the state’s congressional map through Proposition 50, the ballot measure voters approved last November. Gov. Gavin Newsom sold the measure to voters as a way to fight Republican “fire with fire,” abandoning independent redistricting to redraw California’s congressional map in Democrats’ favor (in response to Republicans’ redistricting effort in Texas). The new map was designed to put five of California’s nine Republican-held seats either at a strong Democratic advantage or within Democrats’ reach. The question now is not whether Democrats gain seats here, but how many. And the answer turns on a handful of genuinely competitive races.

Democrats wasted no time turning Trump’s latest inartful phrasing into ammunition. Newsom, who has said he’s weighing a possible 2028 presidential run depending on whether Kamala Harris decides to jump in, led the charge.

“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom posted on X.com. “He is deranged and dangerous.” The governor then directed the State Threat Assessment Center to monitor for threats in case foreign actors interpret Trump’s remarks as an invitation to target California, his spokesman Izzy Gardon said on X.com.

Veteran California Democratic campaign consultant Steve Maviglio said Trump’s remarks were a gift to Democrats just as ballots arrived in the mail this week.

“There’s nothing that stimulates the Democratic base like voting against Donald Trump,” he told RealClearPolitics. “In California where we so greatly outnumber the Republicans, it’s like pouring gasoline on the fire when he comes here or says anything about California.”

Moreover, voter sentiment across the Golden State is generally gloomy. A September poll by the Public Policy Institute of California found that a majority of voters, 54%, believe the state is headed in the wrong direction. Most voters appear to blame federal lawmakers and Trump more than state officials: 76% of those surveyed said they disapprove of Trump’s job performance. Still, only 41% of voters believe the Democratic Party has “a lot” or “some” good ideas, and only 37% said they were ready to embrace Democratic Socialist-identifying candidates.

Republicans are trying to harness that general dissatisfaction and wariness toward far-left candidates. They argue that many of the GOP lawmakers Democrats have targeted are well-known fighters who fit their districts’ more centrist leanings better than the Democrats running against them.

“Californians are done paying more, waiting longer, and living with less safety so corrupt Sacramento and Washington Democrats can protect their socialist agenda,” Christian Martinez, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement.

The scorecard: Dems stand to gain 3 seats, possibly 6 

The arithmetic is simpler than the stakes. Republicans won nine of California’s 52 House seats in 2024. Under the Prop 50 map, only four seats now look safely Republican. That caps Democrats’ realistic prospects as a gain of five.

Winning a total of six of the nine seats previously held by Republicans would require a Kiley defeat. Kevin Kiley, one of the nine, left the Republican Party this year and is running as an independent. If Democrats also unseat him, they will have eliminated six of the nine members who sat on the Republican side of the aisle after 2024.

The Cook Political Report counts only three California races as truly competitive this year: CA-22, CA-13 and CA-48. In 2024, by contrast, California had more closely fought House races than any other state.

Three seats Democrats are counting on

The new map did most of its work before a single ad aired. In California’s northernmost 1st District, Republican James Gallagher won a June special election to replace the late Rep. Doug LaMalfa with about 62% of the vote, but that contest ran under the old lines. The new district trades working class farming cities Redding and Yuba City for upscale Santa Rosa and Sonoma in wine country; Kamala Harris would have carried it by 12 points. Cook rates Gallagher’s November rematch with state Sen. Mike McGuire as “Solid Democrat.”

In the Sacramento suburbs, Kiley’s old 3rd District went from a seat Trump narrowly won to one the Harris-Walz ticket carried by 10 points, and Democratic Rep. Ami Bera moved over to run there.

And in Southern California, Calvert’s redrawn 41st District rounds out the trio. His jump to the 40th costs the GOP a sitting member but not a seat, so the Calvert-Kim fight doesn’t count toward Democrats’ tally. Add those three expected pickups and Democrats sit at three, needing at least one of the remaining battlegrounds to pan out in their favor.

The fourth seat, and the one Trump just made harder

The 48th District is where Monday’s loose presidential talk about Iran might hurt Republicans the most. The open seat stretches from inland San Diego County through Temecula, Hemet, and into Palm Springs. Issa declined to run after the redraw turned his stronghold into a district Harris won by several points, with a roughly 4-point Democratic registration edge. Cook rates it “Lean Democrat.”

Democrat Marni von Wilpert, a San Diego City Council member, has the advantage on paper but not a comfortable one. Jim Desmond has appeared on the ballot in the district’s San Diego portions as a supervisor who is in constant touch with constituents, while von Wilpert has had to introduce herself, and she lives outside the district.

Dems face tough contest in the Central Valley

Rep. David Valadao’s newly drawn district is the only California race Cook rates a true toss-up. On paper it shouldn’t be close: Democrats hold roughly a 16-point registration advantage across parts of Kern, Fresno, Tulare, Kings, and Madera counties, including half of Bakersfield. But Valadao, a dairy farmer and one of the few remaining House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump after January 6, has repeatedly outrun his district. Although he lost the seat in 2018, he won it back in 2020 when Joe Biden carried it comfortably.

His challenger, Randy Villegas, is a populist progressive endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez who beat an establishment-backed moderate in the primary. The race has become a test of whether a candidate well to the left of the old “Valleycrat” mold can win a battleground seat, and whether Villegas, who recently had Sanders visit his district, is too far left for the largely agricultural, though heavily Latino district.

A wild card

Democrats’ gains only count if they don’t give one back. In the 13th District, Democrat Rep. Adam Gray won in 2024 by just 187 votes, the closest House race in the country. Prop 50 helped him by adding heavily Democratic Stockton to the district, and Cook rates the seat “Lean Democrat.” But Stockton is also home turf for GOP challenger Kevin Lincoln, the city’s former mayor, and polling in these low-turnout Central Valley districts has been all over the map but highly reactive to national issues and the president’s negative ratings.

Gray, one of the House’s more moderate Democrats, carries an endorsement from the California Farm Bureau and was one of only six House Democrats to back the deal ending last year’s shutdown.

Then there is Kiley. Rather than face Republican Rep. Tom McClintock in a safe seat, he chose the bluer 6th District in the Sacramento area and is running as an independent against Democrat Richard Pan, a physician and former state senator. Cook rates the seat “Solid Democrat,” and votes for five Democratic candidates combined for nearly 56% in the June primary. Still, a poll from a group backing Kiley showed the race tied, and Harris campaigned for Pan last week, a sign Democrats aren’t taking the 6th seat for granted.

That visit also handed Kiley an opening. Some news organizations, including Sacramento’s KCRA 3, were blocked from covering Harris’ public appearance with Pan on Friday, and a Pan spokesman told KCRA the exclusion also extended to The New York Times.

Kiley pounced. In a campaign blog post titled “The Kamala Debacle,” he wrote that the Harris and Pan camps were openly feuding by day’s end, and he accused Pan’s campaign of a strategy of hiding the candidate. The flap is a small one, but it gave Kiley a press-freedom story line in a week when Democrats were otherwise focused on Trump.

Bottom line: Four is likely, five is a coin flip, six is a stretch

If the Cook ratings hold, Democrats should flip four seats based on the new maps: the three seats the map effectively handed them plus a von Wilpert win in CA-48. Turning five depends on unseating Valadao, a Republican who has survived tougher environments than this one. Six requires beating Kiley too, while holding Gray’s seat in the Central Valley.

With strong well-known Republican candidates facing off in the new districts, Democrats can’t simply count on running the table, Republicans contend.

“California’s House races will decide whether working families keep fighters like David Valadao, James Gallagher, Kevin Lincoln, and Jim Desmond or get more of the same from Democrats who raised costs, left the border wide open, and made communities less safe,” argued Martinez, an NRCC spokesman.

That’s why Democrats are so focused on winning CA-48, and why they were working overtime to capitalize on Trump’s controversial remarks about Iran bombing San Diego and Los Angeles. Whether Desmond’s swift break insulates him – or simply reminds voters which party he belongs to – may decide whether Prop 50 truly slashes the slim GOP congressional representation the state previously had, or further decimates it.
news.summary: 'Democrats can't simply count on running the table'
news.author: RealClearWire,Susan Crabtree

news.title: Trump mocks Kamala Harris’ looks as MAGA women guffaw at rambling Tennessee rally
news.text:
President Donald Trump mocked Kamala Harris’ appearance during a Tennessee rally, sarcastically calling the former vice president “beautiful” as female MAGA supporters standing behind him laughed along with the derogatory crack.

Trump, as he is known to do, appeared to stray from his prepared remarks Saturday at the midterm rally for Tennessee Republican candidates as he recalled campaign rallies held by Harris and former President Joe Biden during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Remember that beautiful Kamala? Somebody said she’s so beautiful. Really?” Trump cracked.

Several women behind Trump guffawed at the remark. One gave Harris a thumbs-down, while another vigorously shook her head.

Trump has repeatedly commented on Harris’ appearance, at times calling her “beautiful” while then insisting he is better-looking than his 2024 presidential election opponent.

During a livestreamed conversation with Elon Musk in August 2024, Trump discussed a Time magazine cover featuring an illustration of Harris and scrutinized her appearance.

“She looks like the most beautiful actress ever to live. Actually, she looked very much like a great first lady, Melania. She didn't look like Kamala,” Trump told Musk. “But of course, she's a beautiful woman, so we'll leave it at that, right?”

Less than a week later, Trump returned to the subject during a rally in Pennsylvania. 

“Don't ever call a woman beautiful, because that'll be the end of your political career,” Trump told the cheering crowd. “But I say that I am much better looking. I'm a better-looking person than Kamala.”

Elsewhere during Saturday’s rally, Trump aired his grievances with his wife, Melania Trump, claiming she disapproves of his speaking style.

“My wife hates when I do this. She says it’s ‘not at all elegant’ and ‘not presidential.’ I said it may not be presidential, but I won the election in a landslide,” he said.

Trump praised Melania as “a very elegant woman” before discussing her documentary, which he claimed was the No. 1 film of the year. 

“And I don’t like that it’s the No. 1 movie. You know why? There’s only room for one star in a family, so I don’t need this movie stuff,” he added.
news.summary: President infamously claimed he was a better-looking person than Harris ahead of the 2024 presidential election
news.author: Erin Keller

news.title: Bernie Sanders Campaigns With Jackson for First Time Since Platner Fallout
news.text: Independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders is campaigning with Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate in Maine’s Senate race, this weekend, his first public appearance in the Pine Tree State since the fallout over Graham Platner’s campaign this summer. Sanders is set to appear at events with Jackson in Bangor, Biddeford and Lewiston in events as Jackson works to motivate the Democratic base to come out to the polls to support him against longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins. It’s one of the most competitive races of the midterms. Maine backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by 7 points in 2024, and Democrats are optimistic about a favorable national environment driven by President Donald Trump’s dwindling national approval rating. But Collins is seen as a formidable candidate who has won by large margins in the past due to her personal popularity and moderate image. Sanders, who caucuses with the Democratic Party, campaigned in Maine with Platner, a progressive oysterman who first won the Democratic nomination back in June. But Platner’s campaign was rattled after he faced sexual assault allegations. He denied any wrongdoing but ultimately dropped out of the race. Some Democrats have taken issue with Sanders for helping to elevate Platner despite what they viewed as red flags about his candidacy. Still, Sanders campaigning with Jackson could be beneficial for the Democrat, Ronald Schmidt, professor of political science at the University of Southern Maine, told Newsweek on Saturday. “The hope is that voters who were enthused by Platner, but who felt disillusioned after his fall might decide to just check out and not participate, that Sanders' appearance will be a way for them to get reconnected to the campaign and to remember what the issues are,” he said. Jackson campaign spokesperson Dan Gottlieb wrote in a statement to Newsweek that the campaign is “excited to welcome Senator Sanders to Maine to rally with Troy Jackson.” “Bernie and Troy know that working people built this country and deserve a government that fights for them. Susan Collins has had nearly 30 years to deliver, and working Mainers are still getting squeezed while she serves the billionaires and corporate interests who bankroll her campaigns,” he wrote. Newsweek also reached out to Collins' campaign for comment via email. Why the Maine Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterms The Maine Senate race is one of the most important of this year’s elections. Democrats are increasingly hopeful about their chances of taking back control of the Senate, and the Maine race is considered to be one of their best chances to flip a GOP-held seat given the state’s Democratic lean. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, so Democrats have to flip four seats to win control of the Senate, as Vice President JD Vance would serve as the tiebreaker in an evenly divided chamber. Being a state that Trump lost three times, Maine is a top pickup opportunity for Democrats. If Democrats fail to flip Maine, their path to a Senate majority would narrow, as they’d have to make up that loss in a more conservative state. Bernie Sanders Boosted Platner Before His Campaign Imploded Sanders was an early Platner endorser, and they campaigned together ahead of the Democratic primary, when Platner easily defeated Governor Janet Mills, who had suspended her campaign earlier in the spring. Platner aligned himself with Sanders on progressive policies including Medicare for All and criticism of foreign wars. Sanders stood by Platner during earlier controversies around uncovered Reddit posts, a tattoo resembling a Nazi symbol, as well as accusations that he engaged in physically threatening behavior during a past relationship, which Platner also denied. Sanders ultimately called for Platner’s withdrawal after the allegation of sexual assault. "I have spoken with Graham Platner about the best path forward for Maine. In light of these very serious allegations, I have recommended that he step aside," he said in a July 7 statement posted on X. The backlash led to scrutiny toward Sanders and other progressives. Schmidt said that while there might be some “bad feelings” toward Sanders over the endorsement, that would pale in comparison to the way Democrats and some independents may feel about Collins. Troy Jackson Leads Susan Collins in New Poll Polling suggests there will be a close race in Maine. On Friday, a new poll from The Washington Post and George Mason University, conducted from September 30 to October 5, showed Jackson up 4 points over Collins, 50 percent to 46 percent, among 800 likely voters. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Jackson also led by 4 points in a recent Marist University poll of 1,505 registered voters from October 1 to 4. Jackson’s support stood at 51 percent, while 47 percent supported Collins in the poll, which had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. But a YouGov/CBS News poll pointed to a head heat, with each candidate’s support standing at 50 percent. It surveyed 1,136 likely voters from September 23 to October 1 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. The outcome of the race is likely to come down to turnout, Schmidt said. Collins is “very, very good at running for reelection,” and Jackson is well-known among Maine Democrats from his time in the state legislature, he said. What Prediction Markets Show Jackson was narrowly ahead of Collins in prediction markets on Saturday, having a 57 percent chance of winning on Kalshi and a 59 percent chance on Polymarket. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Maine Senate Race: Latest Developments Both parties are paying attention to Maine. Former President Barack Obama endorsed Jackson on Friday, potentially giving the Democratic candidate a boost among other Democrats. Trump has also floated the idea of visiting Maine ahead of the midterms in remarks to reporters. Schmidt said that would be “risky” for Republicans. “One of the interesting things about Senator Collins' base of support in Maine is that she's got supporters who are unhappy with the Trump administration, but they give her a lot of leeway in terms of the consequences of her support. She seems fairly well-insulated from voter anger or exhaustion with the Trump administration. But we don't know how far that will go,” he said. Collins and Jackson also faced off during two debates this week, and are again expected to take the debate stage in the coming week for two more debates. One of the most viral moments came as Collins cast herself as a critic of Trump’s tariffs, touting her efforts to obtain relief for products like road salt, which cities in rural Maine import from Canada. Jackson said that minor exemptions did little to offset the broader trade policy implemented by the Trump administration, responding, “We can’t eat road salt.” Like in other states, economic issues such as the high price of home heating oil are expected to play a major role in Maine this year. What Happens Next Two more debates are scheduled for this week on October 13, hosted by WABI and WAGM, and October 15, hosted by News Center Maine, The Portland Press Herald and Maine Public. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.

news.title: Top Dem’s 2028 Plans Hit a Snag Close to Home
news.text:
Kamala Harris faces unlikely pushback if she launches a 2028 bid for the White House: Her husband has reportedly confided that he wants her to let the prospect go. 

Doug Emhoff has privately admitted to others within the former vice president’s circle that he has concerns about another run, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Harris, who lost the 2024 presidential election to Donald Trump after former President Joe Biden dropped out of the race, said last month that she is undecided on whether or not to run again. However, she had also taken some steps towards candidacy, including campaigning alongside Democratic candidates in the midterm elections, and speaking with major donors.

Harris is also the frontrunning Democratic presidential candidate, according to polling from late September, which put her 21 points ahead of her potential rival California Gov. Gavin Newsom. 

However, many of her political allies still refuse to back her: “No thanks,” Iowa’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand told Politico in August. “Let’s move on. We need some new leadership.”

Harris has largely been seen as part of the Democratic establishment that many candidates and voters believe the party needs to move away from. Recent political newcomers, including New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, instead have been seen by some as the party turning over a new leaf. 

“We’ve got a number of younger-generation people who are capable of leading,” Fletcher Smith, a former South Carolina state legislator and one of Biden’s surrogates in the state in 2020, told The Washington Post. “I think what she needs to do is sit out 2028 and let some other people have a shot at saving our democracy.”

The details of Emhoff’s comments around Harris’ candidacy were not reported by The Wall Street Journal, and representatives for Kamala Harris have not responded to the Daily Beast’s request for comment. 

However, Harris still has huge name recognition, as well as significant experience in the White House, meaning that some Democrats still back her. Harris has huge support among Black female voters in particular, a loyal voting bloc that Democrats may not want to jeopardize. 

L. Louise Lucas, the first woman and Black president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate, told The Washington Post that there was “no question” that Black women she knows would see the Democrats’ rejection of Harris as another lost opportunity for a Black female candidate, who they see as having never been given a fair shot.

A potential Harris run could also still significantly shape the Democratic race even if she wasn’t the selected candidate: Gavin Newsom told CNN last month that he wouldn’t run against her in 2028 if she were to launch a bid. “I wouldn’t do that to her,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t waste everybody’s time.”

Harris has recently been focused on campaigning for the midterms, including appearing alongside Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. She also joined a get-out-the-vote call with the Democratic National Committee last week. 

“I do sincerely believe 28 won’t matter if we don’t get through 26,” Harris told voters last month.

news.title: 2026 Zambia General Election Autopsy Part 1
news.text:
By Dr. Field C. Ruwe

The just-ended general election demonstrates a significant departure from the 2021 election, when Hichilema’s landslide electoral victory was internationally lauded as a democratic advancement amid the rise of authoritarian governance in Africa.
In contrast, the August 13, 2026, general election has become controversial following Hichilema’s deployment of the Zambia Army, the loss of a life, allegations of rigging, electoral disputes, a pending judicial petition, and charges of treason against the principal defeated presidential contender, his running mate, and key dissidents. 

This abridged autopsy examines the two principal presidential contenders: Hakainde Hichilema of the UPND and Brian Mundubile, designated bearer for the Tonse Alliance. The report dissects the systematic factors that caused Hichilema’s nail-biting performance. It also deconstructs Mundubile’s bid and illustrates how his late-stage entry created severe vulnerabilities from the outset, which led to the fatal strategic error he committed, potentially altering the election’s outcome.

ZAMBIAN PRESIDENTS AND CHRONIC LOW VOTER TURNOUT 

On August 13, 2026, Zambian voters participated in a presidential election featuring incumbent Hakainde Hichilema and twelve opposition candidates. Electoral records indicate that among the nation’s 22.5 million inhabitants, only 8,786,300 individuals were registered as eligible voters, yielding 4,902,050 valid votes cast. This represented merely 23% voter participation relative to Zambia’s total population, with approximately 17 million citizens abstaining from the electoral process.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) announced on August 18, 2026, that Hakainde Hichilema of the UPND had secured victory amid notably diminished voter participation, garnering 2,965,326 votes, equivalent to 60.5% of all votes cast. His principal opponent, Brian Mundubile, obtained 1,856,222 votes, accounting for 37.8% of the total electoral vote. 

Low voter participation is not unprecedented in Zambia; rather, it has established itself as a persistent pattern dating back to Kenneth Kaunda’s declaration of Zambia as a one-party state in 1973. The 1978 referendum, which presented voters with a choice to either endorse or reject Kaunda’s continuation as the sole presidential candidate for an additional five-year term, engendered widespread dissatisfaction among the electorate and precipitated a notably depressed voter participation rate, with fewer than 40 percent of registered voters casting their ballots.

Since then, scholarly analysis has attributed Zambia’s poor governance and societal stagnation to low voter turnout, as electoral outcomes show here: 1991, Frederick Chiluba (972,605 votes) vs. Kaunda (311,022 votes); 2006, Levy Mwanawasa (1,177,846 votes) vs. Michael Sata (1,170,966); 2011, Sata (1,170,966) vs. Rupiah Banda (987,866); 2016, Edgar Lungu (1,860,877 votes) vs. Hakainde Hichilema (1,760,347); and 2021, Hichilema (2,852,348) vs. Lungu (1,870,780).

The aforementioned data demonstrate that all seven presidents have exercised poor governance. Kaunda demonstrated initial promise, but authority corrupted his leadership. Chiluba engaged in systematic plundering of Zambia’s national wealth. Mwanawasa implemented oppressive governance mechanisms. Banda dismantled the Anti-Corruption Commission. Sata pursued inconsistent economic policies. Lungu accumulated unsustainable levels of debt. Hichilema has demonstrated democratic regression.

Conversely, high voter turnout is found in stable democracies such as Botswana, Ghana, Mauritius, and Namibia, where presidents demonstrate ethical conduct, sustained strategic planning, and advances comprehensive policy approaches that reinforce the vitality of democratic engagement. These nations’ achievements demonstrate strong institutional capacity, independent judicial systems, and forward-thinking administrative practices that align with standards recognized in developed Western democracies.

HICHILEMA DIMINISHING POPULARITY AND DEMOCRATIC BACKSLIDING 

If any African president should serve as a model for African democratic stability in the 21st century, it is Hichilema. His 2021 campaign strategy is widely recognized as an exemplary civic engagement with the electorate within the framework of modern African voting. In 2021, Hichilema executed a “Bally Will Fix It” campaign that felt like the “Singaporean Dream” of third world to first world.

But this time around, the electorate turned on him and used the occasion as a critical referendum on his presidential performance, exposing inadequate governance and questioning the effectiveness of his leadership. As the results poured in, a decline in Hichilema’s political standing became apparent. Suddenly, Hichilema and his UPND were looking like they were the opposition.

What really happened to Hichilema, Africa’s rising star? Power got to his head the minute he received the instruments of power. Suddenly, he saw democracy as an impediment and shifted from his initial reformist promises toward more authoritative approaches. He indulged in nepotism, clamped down on dissent, and enforced stringent cybersecurity laws. His inability to address load shedding challenges and mitigate poverty conditions eroded his public support. Fundamentally, his core agenda was to establish state dominance through the systematic dismantling of the Patriotic Front party (PF).
By the close of 2025, Hichilema had successfully accomplished his objective. The Patriotic Front lacked the capacity to present a viable electoral opposition to the governing UPND. Through such strategies, his first term ended with the comprehensive deterioration of democratic consolidation and a decline in his popularity. 

BRIAN MUNDUBILE AND THE HARRIS EFFECT

Hakainde Hichilema entered 2026 positioned favorably for re-election, given that the Patriotic Front’s ongoing factional disputes had left the opposition without cohesive leadership. However, the situation shifted on January 28, 2026, when Brian Mundubile, a previously obscure former minister from the PF government, stepped into the political spotlight.

From a historical standpoint, presidential aspirants who enter a presidential race late find themselves in a structurally disadvantaged position, especially when they lack pre-existing political stature. Mundubile exemplified this phenomenon. With fewer than seven months to the August election, Mundubile’s path illustrated the formidable challenge that confronted Kamala Harris, who ascended to the head of the ticket three months prior to Election Day following Joe Biden’s withdrawal.
In the lead-up to the election, Mundubile, like Kamala, emerged as a formidable challenger, capitalizing on people’s frustration with poor governance. His campaign initiatives attracted substantial attendance at rallies. This strategy engendered heightened confidence among Tonse Alliance supporters while simultaneously generating considerable apprehension within UPND ranks.

The hurdle was that Mundubile presented certain concerns that merited scrutiny regarding his suitability for the nation’s highest office. To put it candidly, he was not presidential material. His profile fell short of the conventional benchmarks needed for viable presidential leadership. Mundubile lacked the comprehensive policy depth and institutional gravitas traditionally expected of a naturally gifted and persuasive contender. Throughout his public addresses and media appearances, he exhibited an inadequate policy platform, demonstrating a significant absence of preparedness.

MUNDUBILE AND THE BIGGEST BLUNDER 

During the vote counting, the prevailing sentiment throughout Lusaka and the Copperbelt region indicated that Mundubile would emerge victorious. The Mundubile campaign capitalized substantially on the escalating momentum derived from social media spearheaded by Emmanuel Mwamba and other influencers, who communicated favorable positioning within the Mundubile’s internal polling data.

But the mood changed dramatically when some observers began to see striking inconsistencies between presidential and parliamentary results, indicating that votes were being credited to Hichilema’s tally. In a state of panic, Mundubile made a politically ill-advised mistake by delivering a premature national address, wherein he declared: “Our tabulation indicates that we have won this election—We’ve won the election at the presidential level and for the majority of seats in parliament.”
Within the jurisdiction of Zambia, presidential candidates are not granted the statutory authority to independently declare themselves as victors. The exclusive responsibility for validating and consolidating electoral results rests with the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ). Should an opposing candidate prematurely announce electoral success during vote-counting, the act could be interpreted as an attempted insurrection or coup d’état. This context likely explains the deployment of the Zambian military and the prominence of treason allegations in the discourse.

DID HICHILEMA RIG THE ELECTION?
The suspicion of rigging was reinforced by findings from the Christian Churches Monitoring Group, which employed Parallel Vote Tabulation (PVT) methodology to identify a minimum of 30 constituencies whose presidential returns appeared to be artificially enhanced. Also, the suspension of vote counting amplified the concerns. Additionally, political scientists Nic Cheeseman and Nicole Beardsworth examined data released by the ECZ and determined that the election contained substantial deficiencies necessitating a fresh electoral process. Such observations are deserving of a petition.

THE PENDING PETITION
Securing victory through a presidential election petition presents extraordinary obstacles. The judiciary typically functions according to a strong presumption of regularity, meaning it assumes the declared results are valid unless overwhelming evidence proves otherwise. It gets more difficult in an authoritarian state like Zambia, in which the legal system is weaponized as an instrument of state control, regime survival, and political legitimacy.

The judiciary typically functions according to a robust presumption of regularity, whereby the announced outcomes are presumed legitimate unless compelling evidence proves otherwise. This endeavor becomes even more complicated within an authoritarian regime like Hichilema’s, in which the judicial apparatus serves as a mechanism of governmental authority, regime preservation, and political legitimacy.

However, the situation remains promising for Mundubile and the Tonse Alliance. The evidentiary responsibility rests with the petitioner rather than Hichilema. Available information suggests that Mundubile, along with his legal representatives and consultants, has the capacity to present compelling, incontrovertible evidence demonstrating systematic electoral fraud.
During this period of controversy and confusion, the Tonse Alliance should engage qualified forensic investigators to conduct a comprehensive examination of the parliamentary tallies relative to the presidential tallies and compare these figures against the definitive official election data sheets. The Tonse Alliance must ensure the petition precedes the treason trial; otherwise, it will become futile if Mundubile is found guilty of treason or sedition.
[TO BE CONTINUED]

Author is a Doctor of Education and a multicultural researcher affiliated with Northeastern University, Boston, Massachusetts, USA. His most recent published scholarly work appears in the “Pacific Journal” under the title “Phenomenon of Social Media in Sub-Saharan Africa: Leapfrogging From Traditional Communication to Digital Dialogic Communication.”
