news.title: US Midterms: Why Are Women Still Underrepresented In Congress Despite Record Numbers?
news.text:
Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the make-up of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women. Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women.
There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," says Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP) at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers."
Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades.
Also, as Dittmar points out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role: "Stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do."
The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move in to the governor's villa.
House of Representatives: Female Democrats outnumber female Republicans three to one
125 of the 435 representatives in the House are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans.
"There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," says Dittmar. She comments that organizations that specifically recruit, train, and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or non-partisan. Besides, she adds, "A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives.
The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the Speaker or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' Speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023.
US Senate: Even higher bar for women
Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate – 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house.
According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she says. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance. A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts.
For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada.
Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and advisor to conservative politicians.
First black woman state governor?
Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Trump's press secretary during his first term in office.
For the first time in US history, it is possible that a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris's vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia.
Kelly Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007.
But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson.

news.title: Election could be more complicated for Democrats than polls suggest
news.text:
WASHINGTON >> The party out of power typically makes gains in midterm elections. With President Donald Trump unpopular and gas prices stubbornly high, both parties expect Democrats to win seats.

Will it be a blue wave, though? And if so, will it be strong enough to flip both chambers of Congress? Not all waves have the same gravitational force.

In 2006, when President George W. Bush and Republicans faced a backlash over the Iraq War, Democrats flipped 31 seats in the House and five in the Senate, winning both chambers. Bush called it a “thumpin’.”

In 2018, in Trump’s first term, the wave was even larger in House races, with Democrats flipping 41 seats. They failed to win control of the Senate, however, and actually lost two seats to Republicans.

Signs are now piling up that another Democratic wave may be coming. Many officials in both parties privately say they expect Democrats to win back the House, and the main question is how many seats will change hands. The Senate, long seen as easier for Republicans to hold, now appears to be a tossup. Polls suggest the party is playing defense even in states Trump won by double digits two years ago.

Election forecasting is a dangerous business — Republican fortunes could still turn around — but history is often a useful guide. That is why officials in both parties wonder if these midterms will look like 2006, when Democrats flipped both chambers, or 2018, when Republicans were wiped out in House races but picked up two seats in the Senate.

“All these races that are showing we’ve got a 2- or 3-point lead or it’s a tossup, we could end up losing all of them by 2 points,” former President Barack Obama said Wednesday at a fundraiser for Senate Democrats. “It’s within the margin of error.”

Democrats currently face challenges that did not exist in those earlier midterms. Republican redistricting gains have narrowed the House battleground. The party also has a significant cash advantage. Most of this year’s battleground Senate races are in states Trump won easily in 2024. The country has only grown more polarized. And the Democratic Party’s brand remains diminished, with liberal voters mistrustful of its leaders.

“The fact that Democrats allowed Donald Trump to get elected twice is nuts,” said Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., who was first elected in 2018. “We have more on our plate and more to do and more to prove now than we had in 2018.”

Some Republicans, for their part, worry that their messaging this year may not be as effective as it was in 2018.

“Trump is the larger-than-life character in this election,” said former Rep. Steve Stivers of Ohio, who led House Republicans’ campaign committee in 2018. “There’s no Nancy Pelosi on the Democratic side. There are folks trying to use AOC and the DSA, but I’m not sure it has the same knowledge with voters.”

 This time, the economy is worse.

The Iraq War dragged down Bush in 2006, and Trump faced a mass defection of educated suburbanites from his party in 2018. But both years, Americans felt fairly confident about the economy.

That is not the case now.

With gas prices and interest rates up, inflation stubbornly refusing to yield and Trump’s tariffs causing a surge in prices in rural America, the country appears to be seriously angry about the cost of living.

The University of Michigan’s index of consumer sentiment is down 33% since Trump returned to office in early 2025. In May, the index reached its lowest point since it began tracking monthly data in 1952.

“In 2018, people weren’t that sour on the economy,” said former Sen. Heidi Heitkamp of North Dakota, a Democrat who lost her reelection bid that year as rural states turned hard toward Republicans. “They were shocked by the craziness, but they felt pretty good about the economy before the pandemic.”

Trump, she added, “still had much more goodwill than he has right now.”

Republicans have big money advantage

Eight years ago, furious online donors powered a Democratic fundraising surge that Republicans could not match.

Now Republicans have built a huge financial edge that has left Democrats begging for help.

The Democratic National Committee is effectively broke. The party’s House and Senate committees and their allied super political action committees trail far behind Republicans in fundraising. And Trump’s enormously powerful super PAC, funded in part by business executives and corporations looking to curry favor with his administration, has given his party an extra advantage.

The disparity between the parties is perhaps most acute in Texas.

Republican super PACs have directed more than $150 million to help their Senate nominee, Ken Paxton. Democratic super PACs have invested just $4 million so far for their party’s nominee, James Talarico, who has spent more than $60 million of his campaign’s money.

A bad environment is hard to overcome

In just about every midterm election, candidates from the president’s party try to avoid national headwinds by making their elections about local issues.

It rarely works.

Congressional incumbents who have lost in past wave elections compared the experience to struggling through quicksand. Try as they might to dig themselves out from the downward pull of an unpopular president — as some Republicans have recently done by voicing opposition to the war with Iran or questioning immigration raids — the effort is usually futile.

“You can do everything right and if the environment is against you, you’re not going to win,” said former Rep. Chris Chocola of Indiana, a Republican who lost his seat in the 2006 Democratic wave. “You’re not just swimming upstream, you’re almost drowning. There’s not much you can do to extract yourself.”

Senate map is tough for Democrats

Only one of the Senate seats Democrats are trying to flip is in a state, Maine, that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024. The rest — in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas — are in states Trump carried all three times he has run for president.

Former Sen. Claire McCaskill of Missouri, a Democrat who lost in 2018, said her state had shifted toward Trump in 2016 in ways she could not arrest two years later.

“I’ll never forget — in 2016, I was seeing flags and bumper stickers and handmade signs saying, ‘I’m a deplorable,’” McCaskill said. “I remember just thinking, ‘This is different, I haven’t seen this.’ People were anxious to claim him as their guy, and that was still there in 2018.”

Trump has sought to rekindle that connection with Republican voters by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot this year.

Trump is at the center of things

In 2018, most Democrats did not make Trump the centerpiece of their campaigns. They ran instead on healthcare, attacking Republicans for a failed attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act and for cutting taxes for the wealthy.

This time, the president has far less goodwill with voters and has done little to convey that he is concerned about their day-to-day economic concerns.

“Trump was the background music last time, and now he’s much more in the foreground,” said Howard Wolfson, a political aide to Michael Bloomberg, the former New York mayor who directed $112 million to back Democrats in 2018. “You’re seeing more Democratic candidates attempting to tie their opponents to Trump because his numbers are much worse.”

One such Democrat is Roy Cooper, who is leading polls of the Senate race in North Carolina. He released a video last week criticizing his Republican rival, Michael Whatley, for being a Trump acolyte.

Cooper said his opponent was “pretty much going to do and say whatever this president tells him to do and say, regardless of whether it’s good for the people of North Carolina.”

President stumps in deep-red areas

Twenty years ago, Bush was forced to campaign in deeply Republican districts because he would not be helpful to his party’s candidates in political battlegrounds.

Two days before the 2006 elections, Bush traveled to Grand Island, Nebraska, where he sought to motivate rural Republicans to vote in a suddenly competitive House district by celebrating Saddam Hussein’s conviction and death sentence by an Iraqi tribunal.

Trump went to Grand Island on Monday for a rally for Sen. Pete Ricketts, a Republican whose seat had been considered safe. Trump won Nebraska by 20 percentage points two years ago.

Last week, the president rallied in Oklahoma, where he won by 34 points in 2024.

The president’s visits, combined with Republican advertising spending meant to shore up incumbent senators in Kansas and South Carolina, suggest that the political battleground has shifted from traditionally purple states to red ones.

For Republicans like Ricketts and Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, who had expected to cruise to reelection but were now in competitive races, the political whiplash can be severe and put their campaigning skills to the test.

“In 2018, you had people whose districts that were not competitive suddenly becoming competitive,” said Matt Gorman, who was a senior aide on House Republicans’ campaign committee that year. “In a span of a year, they had to go from sitting in a ruby-red district to sitting in a purple district, and that is hard for some people to do.”

Some top donors have also warned her a bid would be a “long shot, according to people familiar with the conversations,” the outlet stated.

“I have not decided if I’m going to run again,” she said at a National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) event in Michigan last month. “I do sincerely believe ’28 won’t matter if we don’t get through ’26.”

In numerous polls the former VP leads by double digits in a hypothetical primary field of Democratic candidates, including high-profile potential candidates like California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY).

However, in the latest Polymarket betting odds, she ranks dead last with only a six percent chance compared to AOC’s 18 percent and Newsom’s 15 percent.

It is a step up from their previous 3,500 square-foot residence in Brentwood, the new home reported as a “mansion” by news outlets, though it falls short of that definition by L.A. and real estate standards.

The former VP hasn’t been languishing in her new Malibu digs, however.

Such moves are typical of a candidate earning favor from a network of state and local politicians who would later come into play as supporters in a presidential bid.

While her husband would prefer Harris does not run, the Journal also reported that “people close to him” fully expect he will support his wife should she decide to make another try at the presidency.

news.title: Trump takes lawsuit against Hillary Clinton to Supreme Court
news.text:
President Donald Trump asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year’s election by linking his campaign to Russia.

The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers for bringing a “frivolous” suit. A U.S. appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions.

Trump’s lawyers wrote in the appeal that Supreme Court review of the case is needed in order to protect the presidency. They wrote that the decisions by the lower courts reflect “a deeply troubling trend of federal courts using sanctions and disciplinary threats to punish the president and his lawyers for legitimate legal positions that those courts (erroneously) reject.”

In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida.

Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a “false narrative” that he and his campaign colluded with Russia. The lengthy suit alleged “racketeering” and a “conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood,” among other claims.

Trump defeated Clinton in that election, despite losing the national popular vote, and served his first term in office from 2017 to 2021.

U.S. government officials have accused Russia of meddling in the 2016 election, and an investigation led by former FBI chief Robert Mueller documented extensive contacts between members of the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in his favor. Trump has called the idea of Russian interference a “hoax.”

Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that year’s election. Trump regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, and has continued to make those false claims.

‘Political manifesto’

U.S. District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump’s lawsuit against Clinton, citing numerous inadequacies, including that Trump waited too long to bring some of the claims. The judge likened Trump’s lawsuit to a “two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him.”

Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and his lead attorney in the case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees and costs, imposing the sanctions for bringing a case that the judge said was intended “to dishonestly advance a political narrative.” The judge also faulted Trump and his lawyers for a “continuing pattern of misuse of the courts.”

Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit used abusive litigation tactics, contained “knowingly false” factual allegations and asserted “frivolous” legal theories.

The Atlanta-based 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge’s rulings in 2025, including the sanctions.

“Many of Trump’s and Habba’s legal arguments were indeed frivolous,” the 11th Circuit stated.

In Friday’s filing, lawyers for Trump and Habba said the time limit for filing the lawsuit should have been extended because he chose to defer suing during his first term in office in order to carry out his constitutional responsibilities as president.

“This court’s intervention is necessary to protect the presidency, and to prevent judicial disagreement from becoming a license to punish its advocates,” the filing stated.

Mueller, serving as a special counsel appointed by the Justice Department, issued a 2019 report on his investigation. The report stated that Russia “interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion,” but also stated that “the investigation did not establish that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities.”

Mueller said in his report that he found “numerous links” and that the Trump campaign “expected it would benefit” from Russia’s effort to tilt the election in Trump’s favor.

Trump’s then-Attorney General William Barr appointed a different special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to look into potential missteps by the FBI.

In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the FBI lacked “actual evidence” to investigate Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and relied too heavily on tips provided by Trump’s political opponents to fuel the probe.

Trump’s Justice Department last year indicted Comey, one of several adversaries of the president hit with criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after he was accused of lying about authorizing leaks to the news media. A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor who Trump handpicked to prosecute Comey had been unlawfully appointed.

Steele, working for an opposition research firm that was hired by a law firm on behalf of the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier that alleged ties between Trump’s campaign and Russia as well as other salacious accusations, all of which Trump denied.
news.summary: President Donald Trump asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year’s election by linking his campaign to Russia.

news.title: The United Auto Workers tries to reassert political power in Michigan as it faces internal divisions
news.text:
SHELBY TOWNSHIP, Mich. (AP) — Walter Usakowski was mowing his lawn in a northern suburb of Detroit when three canvassers from the United Auto Workers approached.

“I don’t even need to talk to you,” Usakowski said. As a retired member, he was already supporting the union’s slate of Democratic candidates in the Nov. 3 midterms.

But he is not sure how many of the other “guys in the shop” will vote for Democrats. He worked at Ford Motor Co.’s Sterling Axle Plant for more than 45 years, and he knows many members who backed Republican President Donald Trump.

The election-year canvassing was one part of the UAW’s efforts to reassert its political power in Michigan, a premier political battleground. Although the union generally backs Democrats, its membership is more divided over which party best represents working-class interests. It also is reckoning with past corruption scandals, a drop in membership and a lack of transparency that has eroded trust within its ranks.

“It’s not going to be an overnight thing,” said JJ Jewell, who is part of the UAW’s Community Action Program executive committee. “Even if this election goes fantastically, that’s not mission accomplished. That means we’re 1% of the way done.”

Internal divisions and distrust pose challenges

Jewell and others made the rounds on a recent sunny Saturday in Macomb County, where Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024. Many of the union members they met in a neighborhood of well-kept suburban houses were retirees, and while most said the cost of living was their top concern, they did not agree on whether Democrats or Republicans would better address it.

One resident, who said she blamed billionaires for the country’s problems, planned to vote for Democrats. Another street over, a couple said they both supported Trump and declined to take a flyer of the UAW-endorsed candidates.

In a microcosm of broader political rifts, union voters remain politically divided. Union voters have traditionally been seen as a Democratic-leaning constituency, but Trump made direct appeals to them with his anti-elite rhetoric and promises to overhaul international trade agreements that sapped factory jobs. In 2024, voters who were union members or were in a household with a union member split between Trump and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris, with more than half voting for the then-vice president and 44% for Trump.

Betty Anderson, a UAW member, thinks the organization is on the right track, but she is not confident about bridging internal political divisions. She said she is angry with members who voted for Trump, whom she sees as selling out the working class.

“I don’t think those people are ever going to be on our side,” Anderson said. “They think they have an opportunity to be in an elite class.”

Leaders hope to rebuild trust with transparency

Since 2017, more than 10 UAW officials have pleaded guilty in a corruption investigation that found millions of dollars of union dues were stolen. Members also faulted leaders for closed-door contract negotiations that they said destroyed trust in the UAW.

Shawn Fain was elected UAW president in 2023 on a platform of transparency, and victories in labor disputes with Detroit’s three major automakers bolstered member support. Leaders hope this will translate into votes for its candidates.

“I think the UAW members now are starting to fall a little more in line,” said Usakowski, the retired axle plant worker.

On Friday, Fain said he won reelection to lead the union for four more years. The results have not yet been certified.

Mark DePaoli, director for one of the UAW’s southeast Michigan regions, said the union hosted forums with candidates where any member could ask questions. The UAW endorsed progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the U.S. Senate primary even though rival Haley Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, worked as chief of staff on an auto bailout task force during the Great Recession, a position she frequently cited while campaigning.

“I don’t think anybody expected us to endorse him,” DePaoli said. In its announcement, the union referenced El-Sayed’s support for universal healthcare and criticism of corporate money in politics. El-Sayed wore a UAW pin during the first Senate debate with his Republican opponent, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers.

“The UAW’s backing of Abdul was critical in winning a historic primary despite being outspent by tens of millions of dollars, and will be just as critical in winning” next month, El-Sayed spokesperson Cole Wozniak said in a statement.

Rogers is emphasizing his opposition to controversial federal regulations under Democratic President Joe Biden that would have required automakers to ramp up production of electric vehicles, which some feared would lead to factory closures.

“Mike knows the challenges our autoworkers face, and he’ll be their champion in the U.S. Senate,” Rogers spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet said in a statement. “The same can’t be said for Abdul and UAW national leadership.”

The union needs to turn out the vote to be politically relevant

Robert Bruno, a professor in the School of Labor and Employment Relations at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said the UAW’s strength relies on its ability to mobilize voters.

“You don’t win campaigns off of your endorsements,” Bruno said. “You win campaigns at the door, or at the bar, or at the union hall.”

In the 1980s, there were more than 600,000 active and retired UAW members in Michigan, according to the union. Today, that number hovers around 350,000. The UAW is still the largest union in the state.

UAW leaders are optimistic after a primary election campaign drive and what they see as better, more transparent leadership. The union said about 113,000 of its members voted early during Michigan’s August primary, and it has volunteers canvassing and calling voters before Election Day.

In September, the UAW hosted a conference of its Michigan political arm for the first time since 2018. Fain told reporters at the Lansing event that the organization wants members to drive the direction of the union, focusing on issues like affordability.

“We are as active as we can be right now,” he said.

GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

news.title: Trump Petitions Supreme Court to Reinstate Lawsuit Against Clinton, DNC, Over Russia Claims
news.text:
President Donald Trump asked the Supreme Court on Oct. 9 to revive his dismissed civil lawsuit against Hillary Clinton, the Democratic National Committee (DNC), and others.

Lower courts rejected the case and ordered Trump and one of his attorneys, Alina Habba, to pay almost $1 million in sanctions. The trial judge and the appeals court called the lawsuit “frivolous,” saying it had no legal merit and appeared aimed at political grievance rather than a valid claim.

Trump is now asking the nation’s highest court to review the appeals court’s decision upholding both the dismissal and the sanctions.

While he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump initiated the lawsuit in federal court in Florida in March 2022, under a federal racketeering law known as civil RICO. That law allows private individuals to seek damages when they claim someone engaged in a pattern of illegal activities, such as fraud or conspiracy.

Trump’s lawsuit touches on topics covered by two earlier government investigations. Former special counsel Robert Mueller’s 2019 report found no criminal conspiracy between the Trump campaign and Russia. Former special counsel John Durham’s 2023 report criticized the FBI’s handling of its 2016 counterintelligence investigation—codenamed Crossfire Hurricane—into possible Trump campaign contacts with Russia. Durham said the FBI relied too much on uncorroborated tips, including material connected to the Clinton campaign.

news.title: Anthony Scaramucci On 'Low Artist' Trump, Misjudged 'Ass-Kissing' And What Really Got Him Fired
news.text:
NEW YORK — Anthony Scaramucci is searching for a video on his phone. A clip that will set the record straight. I’m reading him a quotation from the only White House press conference he gave as President Donald Trump’s communications chief, a period in his life he calls, in his new book, “the 11-day fiasco.”

“I’ve seen this guy throw a dead spiral through a tire,” Scaramucci told a reporter from the briefing room podium, in 2017, when putting on some razzle dazzle in the early-ish days of Trump 1.0. “I’ve seen him at Madison Square Garden with a top coat on, he’s standing in the key and he’s hitting foul shots and swishing them. He sinks 3-foot putts.” (The official White House record was later corrected to “30-foot putts.”)

“I gotta show it to you,” he says, nine years later, while talking at a Manhattan members-only club. “Here we go.”

It’s a video of Trump, in 1992, at a baseball stadium in Buffalo, New York, for a charity event, wearing a notably un-Trumpian plaid shirt. (Scaramucci: “He’s not a fashionable guy.”) Girlfriend Marla Maples is in tow.

Then, history appears to vindicate “The Mooch.” Surrounded by NFL legends, the real estate mogul fires a football through the smallest of holes roughly 20 yards away: more or less, a dead spiral through a tire. The crowd goes nuts.

“I didn’t make it up,” says Scaramucci, who insists he was also at Madison Square Garden for the foul-shot-in-a-top-coat moment. “I don’t have the tape of that,” he adds, sadly.

“They always broke my balls about that,” he says, referencing the mockery he faced for the claims of Trump’s sporting prowess. “But you know what? I saw it.”

Scaramucci does concede, however, that the now infamous peroration was “a gigantic ass-kissing move.” Not that the fawning press conference impressed the big man, who for one day at least was not the center of attention. There was a new showman in town. “He didn’t like it,” Scaramucci says. “One-man show, one spotlight.”

“I shouldn’t have done that,” he says of the exercise in Trump flattery. “Add that to my mistakes, my man.”

Mistakes — his own, but mainly those made by political leaders over the last 30 years — are the centerpiece of his new book, “All The Wrong Moves: How Three Catastrophic Decisions Led to the Rise of Trump,” which attempts to outline “what came before Trump to make Trumpism possible,” and paints a grim picture of the threats to democracy today.

As anyone who has tracked his career over the last decade knows, the Anthony Scaramucci who simped for Trump in the White House for less than two weeks — said to be a modern-day record — and the one who wrote this damning book are appreciably different people.

Scaramucci was once a Trump acolyte who believed the TV personality-turned-insurgent politician was the answer to a malaise created by an out-of-touch bipartisan elite. In the book, he writes how Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told Scaramucci that “I reminded him of his dad, Fred Trump.”

“I said whatever was on my mind; I was classic New York,” he writes of why Trump liked him. The brash Long Island hedge funder, who rocked up to Washington, D.C., in a riot of aviator shades and expensive threads, appeared well-suited to be Trump’s emissary on The Hill.

Now, he is one of the president’s fiercest critics. Scaramucci’s podcast, “The Rest Is History: U.S.”, co-hosted by the BBC’s Katty Kay, is a smash hit, especially in the U.K. Audiences attending an inaugural North America tour this month are likely to hear more unvarnished views on his former boss. 

Scaramucci, 62, who returned to Wall Street after his brief foray in the capital, sees the big mistakes that cleared the way for Trump through the prism of economics. The “money point of view” of history, he calls it.

Put simply, it started with President Bill Clinton’s embrace of trade with China that hurt American workers “deeply, quickly and permanently,” and continued when President George W. Bush cut taxes at the same time as he funded elongated wars in the Middle East. The last gateway to Trump was President Barack Obama bailing out Wall Street after the 2008 crash while main street faced ruin.

The result? Americans, whose wages were crushed while the “fat cats” got fatter, decided to “hire an orange wrecking ball.” Twice.

The book also details his own “catastrophically stupid decision” to work for Trump, first in the 2016 transition team and later as director of communications, as there were “things that he was doing that I morally equivocated on and overlooked.”

“Jeb Bush told me not to. Mitt Romney told me not to,” he says of the two senior Republicans he’d previously raised funds for. “George W. Bush told me not to.”

“But I smelled power, and I got my ego involved,” he adds.

Aside from that bombastic press conference, Scaramucci’s ill-fated 11 days as the president’s media gatekeeper included mopping up after Trump gave a bizarre address to the Boy Scouts of America, which included anecdotes about yacht parties involving “New York’s hottest people.”

“At the Jamboree, Trump speaks for twenty-nine minutes and says almost nothing that’s not completely insane,” Scaramucci writes in the book.

In person, he recalls the horror of standing backstage listening to Trump “lacing his speech with impromptu sexual innuendo to 12-year-old boys,” and senior White House aide Kellyanne Conway explaining this was his problem to deal with.

“And I was like, ’I’m not cleaning that up. I’m giving that to [new press secretary] Sarah [Huckabee Sanders], man. That’s a big elephant shit right there.”

The Boy Scouts speech in West Virginia was the same day his wife — who was in the process of divorcing him — was giving birth to their son in New York, and there was no way of getting back in time. “I mean, it was a really bad day for me,” he reflects.

“Now, some people push back,” he continues. “Oh, you know, you turned [working for Trump] into a great podcast and you did this, did that. It sucked! I’m not gonna sugarcoat it.”

He patched up his marriage and rebuilt his business. But the public humiliation — “getting ripped up by all the late-night comedians” and being “lit up by the fucking ‘Saturday Night Live’ ... calling me human cocaine” — still seems to sting.

He says his downfall came not, as many think, after being caught off-guard in an interview with The New Yorker and saying, among other things, that “I’m not [Trump chief strategist] Steve Bannon, I’m not trying to suck my own cock.” In fact, the president was apparently amused by “one of the funniest fucking things ever said from the fucking White House.”

“You think Trump really gave a shit?” he asks now of the Bannon jibe.

The end, he writes, was fueled by something less profanity-strewn: telling Trump he couldn’t veto the Russia sanctions bill over election interference that Republicans had passed. In any case, after mere days, Scaramucci was fired from the White House by Trump’s new chief of staff, John Kelly. He had “bombed so cataclysmically,” he writes.

Scaramucci initially stayed loyal to Trump. But, by 2019, he recognized Trump “wasn’t ever going to be a blue-collar president. He was exploiting the suffering of the people for his own narcissistic and malevolent ends,” he writes in the book.

Given how Trump expects loyalty, blowback to Scaramucci’s decision to be publicly critical of the president was perhaps inevitable. He’s had that. But Scaramucci points out that Trump “attacked me first,” and then “went after my wife on Twitter, which really caused the fight.” He says MAGA World people, who he was still close to, told Trump he “went over the line with me.”

“By the way, let me tell you something,” he says now. “If Donald Trump attacks your wife, you better back your fucking wife up, OK?”

Trump, he says, is “a low, low artist.”

Despite the feud and his conversion to Never Trumpism, some people are “still mad at me that I went to work for Donald Trump, even though I had my comeuppance.”

“There is a group of people in this country that I will be forever tarred and feathered and tattooed. And then there’s another group of people like, ‘Hey, man, the fucking guy made a mistake. He was honest about it, and he tried to pull us out of it.’”

Does he feel guilty about enabling Trump? “I do feel guilty about it, but I feel like I was exonerated,” he says, countering that he helped President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris to try to stop him. “I feel that I did my duty. And if you’re really being honest, it is the failure of the Democratic Party that he exists, right?”

In the book, Scaramucci argues the second Trump administration’s goal is to have “no effective restraint on the presidency — a kind of ‘soft’ dictatorship” similar to strongman leaders such as Victor Orbán in Hungary and Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

“Democracy has been overcome elsewhere. There’s no magical, existential reason that democracy isn’t being overcome here,” he writes. He also says in the book that “we’ll have to be ready for the next Trump” if we survive this one, and tells me the word from the rubber-chicken dinner fundraising circuit is that Vice President JD Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) are lining themselves up to be his successor, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio may sit 2028 out.

His suggested cure involves codifying many of the “norms” that have failed to constrain Trump, and he advocates for a future president who has the “willpower, guts, and political smarts to drive a stake through” the heart of the Trump playbook. He doesn’t know who that is yet. Also: the Republican Party has to die. “The GOP already has. It’s time for the funeral,” he writes.

In person, he says he doesn’t want to be entirely cynical. He reaches for a suitably Scaramuccian analogy to suggest the president’s current unpopularity, fueled by the Iran war, could mean the midterms are fatal for Trump, vanquishing any fears that he’ll cling to power after 2028 — a kind of Forever Trump, where he refuses to leave the White House despite term limits, which Scaramucci raises as a possibility in the book.

The political cycle means Americans are “stuck with the guy for four years.” But at the end of year two, a “customer complaint aisle” opens: “I believe that he’ll probably get hit with a tsunami of complaints, which could potentially knock him out of business.”

Ted Cruz (R-Texas) are lining themselves up to be his successor, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio may sit 2028 out.

His suggested cure involves codifying many of the “norms” that have failed to constrain Trump, and he advocates for a future president who has the “willpower, guts, and political smarts to drive a stake through” the heart of the Trump playbook. He doesn’t know who that is yet. Also: the Republican Party has to die. “The GOP already has. It’s time for the funeral,” he writes.

In person, he says he doesn’t want to be entirely cynical. He reaches for a suitably Scaramuccian analogy to suggest the president’s current unpopularity, fueled by the Iran war, could mean the midterms are fatal for Trump, vanquishing any fears that he’ll cling to power after 2028 — a kind of Forever Trump, where he refuses to leave the White House despite term limits, which Scaramucci raises as a possibility in the book.

The political cycle means Americans are “stuck with the guy for four years.” But at the end of year two, a “customer complaint aisle” opens: “I believe that he’ll probably get hit with a tsunami of complaints, which could potentially knock him out of business.”

news.title: Anthony Scaramucci On 'Low Artist' Trump, Misjudged 'Ass-Kissing' And What Really Got Him Fired
news.text:
NEW YORK — Anthony Scaramucci is searching for a video on his phone. A clip that will set the record straight. I’m reading him a quotation from the only White House press conference he gave as President Donald Trump’s communications chief, a period in his life he calls, in his new book, “the 11-day fiasco.”

“I’ve seen this guy throw a dead spiral through a tire,” Scaramucci told a reporter from the briefing room podium, in 2017, when putting on some razzle dazzle in the early-ish days of Trump 1.0. “I’ve seen him at Madison Square Garden with a top coat on, he’s standing in the key and he’s hitting foul shots and swishing them. He sinks 3-foot putts.” (The official White House record was later corrected to “30-foot putts.”)

“I gotta show it to you,” he says, nine years later, while talking at a Manhattan members-only club. “Here we go.”

It’s a video of Trump, in 1992, at a baseball stadium in Buffalo, New York, for a charity event, wearing a notably un-Trumpian plaid shirt. (Scaramucci: “He’s not a fashionable guy.”) Girlfriend Marla Maples is in tow.

Then, history appears to vindicate “The Mooch.” Surrounded by NFL legends, the real estate mogul fires a football through the smallest of holes roughly 20 yards away: more or less, a dead spiral through a tire. The crowd goes nuts.

“I didn’t make it up,” says Scaramucci, who insists he was also at Madison Square Garden for the foul-shot-in-a-top-coat moment. “I don’t have the tape of that,” he adds, sadly.

“They always broke my balls about that,” he says, referencing the mockery he faced for the claims of Trump’s sporting prowess. “But you know what? I saw it.”

Scaramucci does concede, however, that the now infamous peroration was “a gigantic ass-kissing move.” Not that the fawning press conference impressed the big man, who for one day at least was not the center of attention. There was a new showman in town. “He didn’t like it,” Scaramucci says. “One-man show, one spotlight.”

“I shouldn’t have done that,” he says of the exercise in Trump flattery. “Add that to my mistakes, my man.”

Mistakes — his own, but mainly those made by political leaders over the last 30 years — are the centerpiece of his new book, “All The Wrong Moves: How Three Catastrophic Decisions Led to the Rise of Trump,” which attempts to outline “what came before Trump to make Trumpism possible,” and paints a grim picture of the threats to democracy today.

As anyone who has tracked his career over the last decade knows, the Anthony Scaramucci who simped for Trump in the White House for less than two weeks — said to be a modern-day record — and the one who wrote this damning book are appreciably different people.

Scaramucci was once a Trump acolyte who believed the TV personality-turned-insurgent politician was the answer to a malaise created by an out-of-touch bipartisan elite. In the book, he writes how Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told Scaramucci that “I reminded him of his dad, Fred Trump.”

“I said whatever was on my mind; I was classic New York,” he writes of why Trump liked him. The brash Long Island hedge funder, who rocked up to Washington, D.C., in a riot of aviator shades and expensive threads, appeared well-suited to be Trump’s emissary on The Hill.

Now, he is one of the president’s fiercest critics. Scaramucci’s podcast, “The Rest Is History: U.S.”, co-hosted by the BBC’s Katty Kay, is a smash hit, especially in the U.K. Audiences attending an inaugural North America tour this month are likely to hear more unvarnished views on his former boss. 

Scaramucci, 62, who returned to Wall Street after his brief foray in the capital, sees the big mistakes that cleared the way for Trump through the prism of economics. The “money point of view” of history, he calls it.

Put simply, it started with President Bill Clinton’s embrace of trade with China that hurt American workers “deeply, quickly and permanently,” and continued when President George W. Bush cut taxes at the same time as he funded elongated wars in the Middle East. The last gateway to Trump was President Barack Obama bailing out Wall Street after the 2008 crash while main street faced ruin.

The result? Americans, whose wages were crushed while the “fat cats” got fatter, decided to “hire an orange wrecking ball.” Twice.

The book also details his own “catastrophically stupid decision” to work for Trump, first in the 2016 transition team and later as director of communications, as there were “things that he was doing that I morally equivocated on and overlooked.”

“Jeb Bush told me not to. Mitt Romney told me not to,” he says of the two senior Republicans he’d previously raised funds for. “George W. Bush told me not to.”

“But I smelled power, and I got my ego involved,” he adds.

Aside from that bombastic press conference, Scaramucci’s ill-fated 11 days as the president’s media gatekeeper included mopping up after Trump gave a bizarre address to the Boy Scouts of America, which included anecdotes about yacht parties involving “New York’s hottest people.”

“At the Jamboree, Trump speaks for twenty-nine minutes and says almost nothing that’s not completely insane,” Scaramucci writes in the book.

In person, he recalls the horror of standing backstage listening to Trump “lacing his speech with impromptu sexual innuendo to 12-year-old boys,” and senior White House aide Kellyanne Conway explaining this was his problem to deal with.

“And I was like, ’I’m not cleaning that up. I’m giving that to [new press secretary] Sarah [Huckabee Sanders], man. That’s a big elephant shit right there.”

The Boy Scouts speech in West Virginia was the same day his wife — who was in the process of divorcing him — was giving birth to their son in New York, and there was no way of getting back in time. “I mean, it was a really bad day for me,” he reflects.

“Now, some people push back,” he continues. “Oh, you know, you turned [working for Trump] into a great podcast and you did this, did that. It sucked! I’m not gonna sugarcoat it.”

He patched up his marriage and rebuilt his business. But the public humiliation — “getting ripped up by all the late-night comedians” and being “lit up by the fucking ‘Saturday Night Live’ ... calling me human cocaine” — still seems to sting.

He says his downfall came not, as many think, after being caught off-guard in an interview with The New Yorker and saying, among other things, that “I’m not [Trump chief strategist] Steve Bannon, I’m not trying to suck my own cock.” In fact, the president was apparently amused by “one of the funniest fucking things ever said from the fucking White House.”

“You think Trump really gave a shit?” he asks now of the Bannon jibe.

The end, he writes, was fueled by something less profanity-strewn: telling Trump he couldn’t veto the Russia sanctions bill over election interference that Republicans had passed. In any case, after mere days, Scaramucci was fired from the White House by Trump’s new chief of staff, John Kelly. He had “bombed so cataclysmically,” he writes.

Scaramucci initially stayed loyal to Trump. But, by 2019, he recognized Trump “wasn’t ever going to be a blue-collar president. He was exploiting the suffering of the people for his own narcissistic and malevolent ends,” he writes in the book.

Given how Trump expects loyalty, blowback to Scaramucci’s decision to be publicly critical of the president was perhaps inevitable. He’s had that. But Scaramucci points out that Trump “attacked me first,” and then “went after my wife on Twitter, which really caused the fight.” He says MAGA World people, who he was still close to, told Trump he “went over the line with me.”

“By the way, let me tell you something,” he says now. “If Donald Trump attacks your wife, you better back your fucking wife up, OK?”

Trump, he says, is “a low, low artist.”

Despite the feud and his conversion to Never Trumpism, some people are “still mad at me that I went to work for Donald Trump, even though I had my comeuppance.”

“There is a group of people in this country that I will be forever tarred and feathered and tattooed. And then there’s another group of people like, ‘Hey, man, the fucking guy made a mistake. He was honest about it, and he tried to pull us out of it.’”

Does he feel guilty about enabling Trump? “I do feel guilty about it, but I feel like I was exonerated,” he says, countering that he helped President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris to try to stop him. “I feel that I did my duty. And if you’re really being honest, it is the failure of the Democratic Party that he exists, right?”

In the book, Scaramucci argues the second Trump administration’s goal is to have “no effective restraint on the presidency — a kind of ‘soft’ dictatorship” similar to strongman leaders such as Victor Orbán in Hungary and Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

“Democracy has been overcome elsewhere. There’s no magical, existential reason that democracy isn’t being overcome here,” he writes. news.title: New polls raise alarms for Trump, Republicans
news.text:
A fresh round of polling is flashing new warning signs for President Donald Trump and Republicans ahead of the midterm elections.

With control of Congress on the line, surveys released this week found Trump's approval rating near second-term lows while Democratic voters reported significantly greater enthusiasm about voting in November. The results come as Republicans confront softening support within Trump's coalition and growing pressure in battleground races.

The numbers are drawing comparisons to 2018, shortly before Republicans lost a sizable margin of support.

Pollster David Paleologos, director of Suffolk University's Political Research Center, noted, "The job approval in October of 2018 was 44%, and he lost 41 House seats," Paleologos said. "Today his approval rating is significantly lower."

More: How Americans rank Trump among US presidents

Democratic enthusiasm rises as Trump's base cools

One of the clearest warning signs for Republicans came from a Reuters/Ipsos survey released this week.

The poll found that only 30% of voters who backed Trump in 2024 described themselves as "very enthusiastic" about voting in the midterms, compared with 48% of voters who supported former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The survey also suggests many motivated voters are driven more by opposition to Trump than support for him. Among highly enthusiastic voters, 62% said they were eager to vote against the president, while 36% said they were excited to support him.

Pew Research Center survey also pointed to erosion within Trump's own coalition. The poll found that 67% of his 2024 voters approve of his job performance, down 28 percentage points from the start of his second term.

The survey also found growing unease among Republicans. Just 39% said they were satisfied with the direction of the country, down from 65% at the start of Trump's term and the lowest level recorded during his second presidency.

Republicans face difficult choices

As Election Day nears, some analysts are watching where Republicans choose to spend their money.

Paleologos said party leaders may soon be forced to focus resources on their most competitive races.

"What you're going to see in the next seven to 10 days is the big money, the Republican National Committee, starting to pull money out of states," Paleologos said. "That's going to be a culture shock for some of these Republican Senate nominees."

There are already signs of shifting priorities. According to Associated Press reporting, Republicans recently moved money from North Carolina's Senate race to Kansas as the fight for Senate control enters its final weeks.

The shift comes as polling has tightened Republicans' path in both states. An East Carolina University survey found former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper leading Republican Michael Whatley by seven points, while a YouGov poll showed Democrat Adam Hamilton ahead of incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall by three points in Kansas.

Another rough week of polling for Trump

Those concerns come amid another rough week of polling for the president.

Pew's survey released Oct. 8 found that only three in 10 Americans approve of Trump's job performance, marking a new second-term low and leaving him just one point above his lowest rating at the end of his first term.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll released earlier in the week found Trump's approval rating at 32% for a second consecutive week, matching the lowest level the pollster has recorded for him across both of his terms in office.

What polling averages show

Individual surveys vary, but major polling averages point to the same conclusion: Trump remains deeply underwater with voters heading into the final weeks before the midterms.

As of Oct. 9, averages from RealClearPolitics, The New York Times and Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin all showed Trump's approval rating in the high 30s and his disapproval rating around 60%.

While those averages are higher than some recent polls, they underscore the challenge Republicans face as they try to hold Congress in a political environment where more Americans disapprove than approve of the president's performance.

Contributors: Terry Moseley, USA TODAY

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

news.title: After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help
news.text:
Democrats lost the 2024 elections in part because of their eroding support among Latino voters, a constituency that was once a reliable segment of their base.

That November, Kamala Harris won the Latino vote by three points, according to the Pew Research Center. In 2020, Joe Biden carried them by 25 points.

This year, swing districts with large Hispanic populations could help decide which party controls the House. And Democrats are scrambling for ways to win those voters back.

One new effort comes from the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, also known as BOLD PAC. In February, they launched a program to personally connect social media influencers with voters.

"We're turning to trusted voices in local communities that have followings giving them information and then allowing them to create content in a way that is organic and authentic," said Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., who chairs BOLD PAC.

That includes Latina content creator Alexa Flores, who not long ago mostly posted about beauty tips and fashion. But the Arizona resident shifted to politics in response to the Trump administration's immigration policies.

She says she wants Latino voters to understand their impact if they vote.

"My job is to get people to understand that so that they can go and move that needle," said Flores, who has nearly 500,000 followers across her platforms.

Her job now includes "get-out-the-vote" events with BOLD PAC in swing districts around the country. Flores, for her part, will appear at a wine tasting event in Las Cruces, N.M. – where Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez is locked in a close race against Republican Greg Cunningham. She'll also appear at a Día de los Muertos event with lowriders and voters in Tucson, Ariz., where Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza is trying to unseat GOP incumbent Juan Ciscomani.

BOLD PAC says it is not paying content creators for posts. Instead, they're providing stipends of $1,500 for flights, hotels and other travel costs for each event. 

Sánchez says content creators could help bridge a gap for her party. Thirty percent of Latinos regularly get their news from influencers on social media, according to Pew Research Center. That's more than any other demographic.

"So whether that's ... Instagram or YouTube or TikTok, that's how they're getting their information," she said. "So we need to be in those spaces."

Democratic strategist Stephanie Valencia says Democratic efforts to win back long term support from Latino voters is going to be an uphill battle. Valencia is co-founder of Equis Research, which estimates that roughly a third of Latinos are considered independent voters.

Of those, more than 40% think neither party cares about people like them. 

"One election cycle is not going to solve the problem that Democrats have had and a frayed trust with Latino voters that has developed over the last several election cycles," Valencia said.

In 2024, Latinos shifted right in response to what they saw as liberal immigration policies and a focus on foreign intervention over domestic policy under former President Biden. That year, President Trump grew his party's share of Latino votes by double digits to 48%, leaving Democrats with a slim majority, according to Pew Research Center.

It's those kinds of swings that can cost a party a close election.

This year, leaders at BOLD PAC sense an opportunity, as they've watched a growing number of Latinos say they feel betrayed by President Trump's immigration and economic policies.

Still, Valencia warns that some Democratic campaigns continue to underestimate how "swingy" a good chunk of the Latino electorate is. That is, they show up with too little, too late when it comes to campaign spending and messaging.

"Latinos are just a more persuadable universe and can't just be treated as a base turnout universe for Democrats," she said.

Solangie Hernandez Hollowell, a Texas influencer who is also working with BOLD PAC, agrees. Like others, her posts often don't even mention specific candidates, but they do focus on issues that Democrats are campaigning on this cycle – issues like taxes and immigration.

So she wants to help Latinos connect with candidates in a way that goes beyond the transactional.

"Latinos feel like politicians show up just right before the election. I don't feel like we feel very heard," she said.

So she's translating what this political moment can mean for them.

"My main goal right now is making sure that everything that's happening around the world reaches my family and my community in a way that they can understand it," she said.

Flores, the Arizona influencer, says she hopes for more awareness that Latinos are having a growing impact on major pieces of American life.

"The wave of Latinos growing in this country is becoming a bigger voice for a lot of things," she said.
news.summary: Democrats are hoping to win back Latino voters who have soured on both parties. They hope Latino content creators will bridge the gap.
news.author: Claudia Grisales

news.title: Trump Takes 2016 Election Conspiracy Battle Against Hillary Clinton To Supreme Court
news.text:
President Donald Trump has asked the US Supreme Court to revive his dismissed lawsuit accusing Hillary Clinton, James Comey and others of conspiring to link his 2016 campaign to Russia.

A federal judge dismissed the case as frivolous and ordered Trump and his lead lawyer, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in legal fees and costs.

The 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal and sanctions in 2025, faulting Trump and his lawyer over several frivolous legal arguments.

Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation found extensive Russian interference in the 2016 election but did not establish that Trump’s campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in those activities.

October 10, (THEWILL) – US President Donald Trump has asked the Supreme Court to revive his dismissed lawsuit accusing former Democratic presidential candidate, Hillary Clinton, former FBI Director, James Comey, and other political opponents of conspiring to undermine his 2016 presidential campaign by linking it to Russia.

Trump filed the appeal on Friday, challenging lower court rulings that dismissed the lawsuit and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against him and his lead lawyer, Alina Habba, for pursuing what a federal judge described as a frivolous case intended to advance a political narrative.

THEWILL recalls the lawsuit, filed in 2022 after Trump left office following his defeat by Democrat, Joe Biden, in the 2020 presidential election, accused Clinton and her allies of orchestrating a scheme to discredit his campaign by promoting what he called a false narrative of collusion with Russia.

The complaint, lodged in a federal court in Florida, named Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer, Christopher Steele, the Democratic National Committee and several other individuals and organisations.

Trump alleged that the defendants conspired to damage his political prospects ahead of the 2016 election, when he defeated Clinton despite losing the national popular vote.

The lawsuit included claims of racketeering, conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood and other alleged legal violations.

The Republican president has repeatedly described investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 election as a political hoax and has maintained that his campaign was unfairly targeted.

Judge Calls Lawsuit A Political Manifesto

US District Judge, Donald Middlebrooks, dismissed Trump’s lawsuit, citing numerous legal deficiencies, including the fact that Trump had waited too long to bring some of the claims.

In his ruling, Middlebrooks likened the complaint to a “two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him.”

The judge subsequently ordered Trump and Habba to pay nearly $1 million in legal fees and costs, concluding that the lawsuit was intended “to dishonestly advance a political narrative”.

Middlebrooks also faulted Trump and his legal team for what he described as abusive litigation tactics, knowingly false factual allegations and frivolous legal theories.

The judge characterised the case as part of a continuing pattern of misuse of the courts.

Trump and Habba challenged the decisions, but the Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal and sanctions in 2025.

“Many of Trump’s and Habba’s legal arguments were indeed frivolous”, the appeals court stated.

In subsequent court filings, lawyers for Trump and Habba argued that the lower courts’ decisions were having a “profound impact on the presidency, and the nation as a whole.”

Their latest appeal seeks to persuade the Supreme Court to intervene and allow the lawsuit to proceed despite the adverse rulings.

Mueller Report Documented Russian Interference

The legal dispute is rooted in the controversy surrounding Russia’s alleged efforts to influence the 2016 US presidential election.

Mueller, appointed by the Justice Department as special counsel, issued his report in 2019 after investigating Russian interference and possible links between Moscow and Trump’s campaign.

The report stated that Russia “interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion.”

It also documented numerous links between Russia and individuals associated with Trump’s campaign, noting that the campaign expected to benefit from Russia’s efforts to influence the election.

However, Mueller stated that his investigation did not establish that Trump’s campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities.

Trump has repeatedly cited that finding to reject allegations of collusion, while describing the broader investigation as politically motivated.

In 2019, Trump’s then-Attorney General, William Barr, appointed another special counsel, John Durham, to investigate potential misconduct by the FBI in its handling of the Russia inquiry.

Durham’s 2023 report concluded that the FBI lacked “actual evidence” to investigate Trump’s 2016 campaign and relied too heavily on information supplied by Trump’s political opponents.

The findings became central to Trump’s argument that the investigation was improperly initiated and politically driven.

Clinton Campaign, Steele Dossier At Centre Of Dispute

Steele, a former British intelligence officer, compiled a dossier containing allegations about links between Trump’s campaign and Russia while working for an opposition research firm hired by a law firm acting on behalf of Clinton’s campaign and the Democratic National Committee.

The dossier also contained other controversial allegations about Trump, which he denied.

The material became a major source of controversy during and after the 2016 election, with Trump and his allies arguing that it helped fuel an effort to discredit his campaign.

Clinton and the other defendants were accused in Trump’s civil complaint of participating in a broader effort to damage his political standing. Those allegations were rejected by the lower courts, which dismissed the case.

The lawsuit’s dismissal and the financial sanctions against Trump and Habba have since become separate points of contention in the legal battle.

Trump returned to the White House in 2025 after defeating Democratic candidate Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. He has continued to challenge investigations and legal actions involving his political opponents and his first presidential campaign.

His latest appeal seeks to reopen a case that lower courts concluded was legally deficient, renewing the dispute over the origins and handling of the Russia investigation.

news.title: Burri i Kamala Harris nuk dëshiron që ajo të kandidojë përsëri për presidente
news.text:
Bashkëshorti i ish-nënpresidentes amerikane Kamala Harris, Doug Emhoff, u ka thënë privatisht disa personave se do të preferonte që ajo të mos kandidonte sërish për presidente të Shteteve të Bashkuara, sipas personave të njohur me bisedat, raporton WSJ.

Ndërkohë, disa donatorë demokratë i kanë shprehur drejtpërdrejt Harris shqetësimet e tyre, duke e cilësuar një kandidim të mundshëm si një sfidë të vështirë politike.

Harris nuk ka vendosur ende nëse do të hyjë në garën presidenciale për herë të tretë. Megjithatë, lëvizjet e saj të fundit kanë shtuar spekulimet për një rikthim të mundshëm në garën për Shtëpinë e Bardhë.

Ajo ka zhvilluar biseda me donatorë të rëndësishëm, ka punësuar staf dhe ka udhëtuar në shtete kyçe për të mbështetur kandidatët demokratë përpara zgjedhjeve të mesit të mandatit, që do të mbahen në nëntor.

Këto zhvillime po mbajnë të hapur mundësinë e një kandidimi të ri të Harris, ndërsa brenda rrethit të saj politik duket se ekzistojnë pikëpamje të ndryshme për këtë çështje.

Ish-nënpresidentja ende nuk ka bërë një njoftim zyrtar për kandidaturën e saj të ardhshme presidenciale./ CNA
